Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There occurs today one of those happy parliamentary occasions when we wish to pause briefly to do honour to one of our own. I refer of course to the birthday of the right hon. the Prime Minister. It appears that all hon. members wish to join me in extending to him and to Madame St. Laurent our most heartfelt congratulations together with our best wishes for continued health and happiness and, of course, many happy returns of the day.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is indeed an historic occasion, being the second time since confederation that a prime minister while in office has attained the age of 75 years, the other being of course the founder of this country, Sir John A. Macdonald. This is one occasion that permits parliament to reveal its glory which consists in the fact that the sentiments that separate us on different sides of the house are not as great as the sentiments that join us together. On behalf of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, and I am sure on behalf of all members of the house, I extend warmest congratulations and felicitations to the Prime Minister, coupled with the hope that he may enjoy many more years of good health and much happiness.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the leader of this group (Mr. Coldwell) and all my colleagues I should like to join with Your Honour and the other members of the house in heartiest felicitations to the Prime Minister on his birthday. We are glad to see him looking so well and wish him many happy returns. I am sure he will understand if I add that we feel that surely the time has come for him to enjoy a very happy retirement.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure I speak for all my colleagues when I say we are delighted to see the Prime Minister enjoying such good health and living in such vigorous fashion on this
his 75th birthday. I had thought during the past few months that he must have found the fountain of youth and it was in my mind to ask him privately some time just what it was and where I could find it but I was afraid he might suggest to me that I join the Liberal party and then I would find it. Seriously, I do want to join with others in extending to the Prime Minister our heartfelt felicitations, our good wishes and to express the hope that he will enjoy many more years of vigour, good health and usefulness in whatever calling he may follow.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you and, through you, all the members of this house for the great satisfaction your words and the way in which they have been received give one when he passes another milestone after a considerable number that have been passed in previous years. To the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and to those who speak for other groups in the house I wish to express my complete agreement with their stated opinions this morning that though there are many things upon which we disagree and upon which we express our disagreement in this forum, there is no doubt that much stronger and more impressive than the divergences which arise in our opinions and in our expressions is the sentiment that we are all Canadians and all doing our best here to serve our fellow Canadians. That, I am sure, is the solid basis of the personal friendships which exist between the members of this house and of the sentiments which are expressed on every occasion when it is the turn of any one of us to be passing one of the milestones in his life. I am really happy to be of the group that thus in friendship, each to the best of his ability, strives together to serve our fellow Canadians.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) wishes me years of happy retirement. I feel that I shall be happier as long as I do not have to reach the point where retirement would be the wisest decision to make. It was felt in the garden of Eden that the condemnation to earn one's bread by the sweat of one's brow was a real condemnation. That was long ago. I think the greatest satisfaction we get out of life now is that of doing useful work to the best of our ability.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR PERFORMANCE OF MUSICAL RIDE IN UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement in respect of an announcement being made in Great Britain.
Last summer a number of the most prominent agricultural societies in the United Kingdom requested through the Department of External Affairs that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police musical ride be made available for presentation at selected agricultural fairs and other events there during the summer of 1957. The government has agreed to this and accordingly the ride will be going to the United Kingdom this coming spring.
[Mr. St. Laurent (Quebec East).)
This well-known and distinctly Canadian attraction consists of 32 mounted men under command of an officer. There are also included a senior N.C.O. riding master, a band conductor, and two to four spare riders. On December 3, 1956, a series of musical ride engagements in Canada and the United States was completed. These engagements were widely acclaimed as outstanding and those presented in the United States brought, I am sure, a great measure of credit to this country. The troop going to the United Kingdom will be composed of substantially the same personnel.
At a recent meeting of the royal agricultural society of England delegates expressed their gratitude and warm appreciation to the Canadian government for its generosity in making the Royal Canadian Mounted Police musical ride available in the United Kingdom this summer.
Although no definite itinerary has been arranged as yet, it is understood that the committee in the United Kingdom which is co-ordinating arrangements has received applications from 10 of the largest and best known agricultural societies for the appearance of the ride at their annual exhibitions. As an indication of the interest and enthusiasm back of the invitation, one of the royal agricultural shows has in mind slanting its whole program towards Canada provided our ride can be featured.
The troop will receive its Anal training at the Rockcliffe barracks during the early spring and travel by ship to a United Kingdom port towards the end of April.

Would he also say whether or not in either or both of these resolutions there will be any mandatory requirement imposed upon Egypt to assure that the Suez canal will be open to the traffic of all nations, including
Supply-External Affairs Israel? After all, if we in Canada are tc>
be asked to make a loan for a project there should be some assurance that in the event the project is proceeded with it will not be only a temporary clearing of the canal to-be followed immediately by acts of sabotage on the part of Nasser and those associated with him.
On the basis of the information which only the government can have, would the minister say what the probabilities are whether or not Canada's representatives at the United Nations are now convinced that Nasser's future course will be a reversal of his previous course with regard to the canal? Certainly if the loan is made and the work proceeded with and it merely provides another opportunity for Nasser to destroy the usefulness of the canal and thereby make his contribution to preventing the free world from using the canal, a loan such as this will be worthless.
There is something more too in connection with the loan. What is the basis upon which the government contends that repayment will be made? Nothing very clear has been said in that regard yet. I know of no provision under the United Nations for the borrowing of money and I am wondering how provision will be made or what the plan is to assure repayment.
Finally, I repeat the question to which we received no answer the other day. What is Canada's attitude going to be now that she has taken a greater interest in the Middle East situation and in particular the Suez canal situation than the defence minister revealed in August last when he said Canada had no interest in the Suez dispute? What is Canada's attitude going to be with respect to securing repayment by compensation being demanded from Nasser?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must repeat the point of order I raised on Wednesday that this item is confined solely to a loan for the purpose of clearing the canal and should not give rise to a debate about other matters, particularly other matters which are under discussion at the United Nations at the present time. I am quite prepared to answer direct questions affecting the loan and the attitude that Canada is prepared to take and is taking with respect to the canal itself, but I submit with great respect that other general questions are out of order.
The first question directly affecting the loan is the method of repayment. I have made it quite clear on at least two occasions in the course of the debate-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Not very clear.

Supply-External Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Permit me to complete the
sentence. I have made it quite clear that it is an advance by this country for the purpose of expediting the clearing of the canal. It is a loan in the sense that we expect to receive it back in either one of two forms, either by repayment should some form of financing other than the present one be undertaken by the secretary general of the United Nations or if an assessment is ultimately made by the United Nations on the nations, including Canada, for the cost or a part of the cost of the clearing of the canal this payment will be credited to any such assessment as may be levied on Canada. If it happens that Canada's assessment is less than $1 million we will then have a repayment made to us out of any funds that the secretary general of the United Nations may be able to raise for the purpose of completing the clearing of the canal.
I do not suggest the probability of having this sum repaid to us within a matter of days or weeks. I think the probability is that the second alternative will be the one that will be acted upon, namely, that when the cost of the job is assessed among the members we will receive a credit and a refund should our assessment not total $1 million.
It is true, as the Leader of the Opposition said, that the United Nations does not have the necessary means of borrowing money and, as a matter of fact, that is why an appeal was made to Canada, among other countries, to provide money in this, may I put it, informal manner in order that the various salvage companies might have funds from time to time to pay wages and costs.
The second question directly related to the financing is the question of what the position will be with respect to Nasser arid his attitude towards the canal when the canal is finally cleared. I think that everyone knows perfectly well that we cannot project in our own minds what the Egyptian government may do two or three months from now. This is a calculated risk that I think we are bound to take arid I believe that hon. members opposite are prepared to take it.
It may well be that the present Egyptian government will continue to be as unco-operative with regard to some things as they have appeared to be up to the present time. But it is not the custom to refuse to take action if you cannot really see the end of your action. It is true that you must be careful about it and take all the precautions you can, but the problem is not whether we should lend the money now in the certain knowledge that in three months' time Nasser and his government will take a certain attitude towards the canal. The problem we

have to face is, should the canal be cleared at the present time, what means should be adopted to do that, and then let us try to work out the means whereby the canal will be, as I have already said, free to the use of all nations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is he showing any signs
of co-operation now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: So far as our knowledge goes, his attitude is reflected in the statements he has made and perhaps semi-officially in the statements made by the press of his country. One can interpret those attitudes in whatever way he thinks they should be interpreted.
Can the minister tell us briefly what they are?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The only recent statement about which we have information is the one which I think would be put well down the list of official statements which was read the other day by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. The press in Egypt has, of course, been conducting a campaign which would not lend itself to co-operation and compromise at this time anyway. But that is not to say that this will be the continuing attitude of the Egyptian government. Indeed, if the canal were cleared by the United Nations and if at that time the Egyptian government were informed by the United Nations to this effect: "We have undertaken this task; we have expended the sums of money with or without a final settlement of how the money is to be collected and we expect the canal to remain open now to the shipping of any nations free of any discrimination", we would hope, of course, that at that time the collective pressure of the United Nations would be sufficient to ensure that Nasser would not attempt to interfere with shipping in the canal.
May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Has he any ground for believing that Russia would join in the pressure on Nasser?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think that would be too broad a statement to which to make a direct answer. However, I think it would be correct to say that there have been occasions, both in the United Nations and in public negotiations with other countries, when it has been indicated that Russia-with all the difficulties that we have recognized in our diplomatic relations with that country-nevertheless is as conscious as is any one of the possibilities which might ensue if a peaceful settlement were not arrived at of any particular problem. The

solution may not be satisfactory. It may only be a compromise of a good many interests and it may be a subject of irritation. I would hope that we would not find that world peace would be permanently jeopardized by a question such as whether or not the ships of all countries should have free access to the canal when it is cleared in two or three months time.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Is it not true that England and France offered to clear the canal free of any assistance from other nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What they offered was to be of assistance in clearing the canal and that offer has been accepted to the extent that some British and French groups are working on it. My understanding is that at least one of them-if not both-is doing it without charge.
May I ask this question? Did not the British parliament the other day vote a sum of money for the clearance of the canal in the amount of some $39 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have not been informed that was the case. I would be surprised if it were because that would represent almost the total cost of clearing the canal.
That report was in the press.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should be glad to see the report. Our last information is that the $10 million that was referred to at the beginning of this debate is still needed for the purpose upon which we base the request to parliament.

May I ask
another question before you proceed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Has this government already paid any of that money over to the United Nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. We have paid no money at all to the United Nations in connection with this matter. I think my hon. friend is probably confusing this with the money we paid in connection with Hungarian refugees; I refer to the $1 million we paid in November for that purpose.
If I have not answered these questions directly, I should be glad to be prompted. I think hon. members will realize the impossibility of giving any assurance except that the government will use its best endeavours and the best possible diplomatic approach
Supply-External Affairs that we can make through the United Nations and through other sources, in order that in the time that will elapse between now and the completing of the clearance of the canal we shall have, if not direct assurance, at any rate acquiescence in the use of the canal unrestrictedly by other nations and subject of course to the conditions of the treaty and the rights of those who claim rights in the canal. This will be a matter of great debate, no doubt, at the United Nations during the next two or three months.
I do not think there is any difference of opinion at the moment in this house about what our attitude ought to be in the course of those negotiations. As I said the other day, I think that everyone believes that you are more likely to get peaceful solutions if your country is in good shape. The economy of Europe has been suffering because of the blockage of the canal. When people are spending money in higher taxes, higher costs for gasoline and the like, when they are put on quotas and rations and the like, it is far better to get them off those things at the earliest possible time not only for their own sake but for the sake of a state of mind in which one could make more suitable settlement of the difficulties that gave rise to the restrictions on them.
It has been a surprising thing perhaps to most hon. members that, since this trouble began, the price of sterling has strengthened. I would not suggest that it should not do so. However, a great many people looked forward to certain financial difficulties in Europe this winter, which difficulties are taking place but which are being met by the peoples there in a spirit which has maintained confidence in the currencies of those countries. I would not ascribe a reason for that. I merely report it. But even so, let us consider how much better those currencies would be and how much better the feeling of the people would be if their costs were cut and if they were put back in the position which they occupied before the difficulty with regard to the canal. While a political settlement of the difficulty is, of course, a most desirable end, I suggest that an economic solution to the problem is urgently needed; and I know that fact is appreciated by hon. members who, in the main, I think will agree with this vote.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the minister is being extraordinarily optimistic when he speaks as though all that is required to bring about an economic solution is for this money to be put up and then for the canal to be cleared. I am afraid that is just the beginning of the problem. The minister himself today has in effect admitted that there is absolutely no assurance that, the minute the canal is cleared, this dictator

Supply-External Affairs Nasser will not take the position that British, French and Israeli ships cannot use it. Of course the minister cannot go any further than the actual facts of the case warrant. But I understand from him that that is the position, namely that the free world has absolutely no assurance that Nasser will allow the shipping of those three nations or for that matter the shipping of any other nations to use the canal once the money has been spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is correct.

I think that shows just how terribly serious this question is and the need for the Canadian government and the governments of the other freedom-loving countries to take a determined stand that this sort of nonsense is not going to be permitted any longer. May I ask the minister, for example, whether this question of free navigation of the canal is even under consideration in the debate now taking place in the United Nations? When the Prime Minister spoke on Wednesday he intimated to us that the whole position from Canada's point of view was covered by the speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on January 29 in New York. We have now had an opportunity to read that speech. In it I find not one word about the Suez canal or about the question of navigation. May I ask the minister whether or not that is the fact, that all the discussions now taking place do not involve at all the question of the clearing of the canal or the free navigation of it?
Then, one other question I would ask him. Is there any move under way to use the United Nations emergency force as a police force in the Suez canal area as distinct from the Sinai desert, the Gaza strip and the gulf of Aqaba, to ensure that there is free navigation of the canal? Apparently, from all we can see, there is not any such intention. No nation seems to have mentioned it at the United Nations in the course of this debate, and yet I do not know of any other way in which the free navigation of the canal will be assured. I should like to know the opinion of the Canadian government as to whether or not this force should be given the task of policing the Suez canal itself until agreement has been reached under which there will be free navigation of the canal by the ships of all countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I shall try to answer both questions, Mr. Chairman. The first had to do with navigation, and whether it was under debate, and the second had the same purpose. I think my hon. friend misunderstood the Prime Minister the other day. You may remember that at the time I raised the same point of order that I have now mentioned

again. The Leader of the Opposition had asked about the Gaza strip and other related matters in connection with the dispute between Israel and her neighbours, and it was that to which the Prime Minister was referring when he said that the attitude of the Canadian government could be gleaned from the speech which was made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Prime Minister had in mind that it was that part of the question which had been addressed to him that would be covered by that speech. There was no intention to suggest that in the speech there was a discussion of the particular matter we are now discussing, namely, the canal itself, although I think my hon. friend will agree with me, having read the speech, that there were direct references to the gulf of Aqaba and other matters that stem a little bit from the canal clearing.
But nothing about the canal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, I agree. The Prime Minister did not intend his answer should be taken in that light. He intended his answer to refer to those questions having to do with Israel and the Gaza strip which had been asked of him, and not to the canal itself. It was for that reason, as a matter of fact, that at that time I raised, as I raised again this morning and raise now, the point of order that we ought to confine our discussion to the canal rather than the Gaza strip and other matters that have arisen out of this but are not subjects we are discussing at the moment.
The second question has to do with the use of the United Nations emergency force in connection with the canal itself, and whether or not that is under discussion at the present time. I think my hon. friend should bear in mind the priority at the moment at the United Nations. At the moment, they are discussing the question of Israel, the Gaza strip and matters connected with whether or not Israel should withdraw and what should take the place of the Israeli forces should that withdrawal occur. The other question, the question of the canal and what happens to it after it has been cleared, will be discussed on the motion which will try to allocate the cost of clearing amongst the various members of the United Nations or in whatever manner may be decided.
At the moment, however, this subject is not under consideration because, as I say, the United Nations feels this other matter should have priority of consideration. As I said a moment ago, I am sure it will be raised during this session and at that time

there will be no point of order raised if discussion goes on about the canal and not about the Gaza strip.

This is a discussion about the canal. The Canadian taxpayer is being asked to put up a million dollars to help clear that canal. Now, what is the stand of the Canadian government with regard to the use of the United Nations emergency force in the canal area in order to ensure that there will be free navigation for the ships of all nations? This must have been considered by the Canadian government. If it has not, it should have been because I believe that on November 2 there was a resolution adopted in the general assembly of the United Nations which authorized action to reopen the canal and this is the important part of that resolution to which I wish to draw attention and to secure full protection of navigation. The Minister of National Health and Welfare will correct me if I am wrong in that statement. The resolution of the assembly itself deals not only with the clearing of the canal but also with the free navigation of that canal.
Does the Canadian government believe, or does it not, that the United Nations emergency force should be used in the canal area itself until agreement has been reached which will ensure that all ships can use that canal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I thought I dealt directly with the question on Wednesday, so I shall quote myself by reading two or three sentences found on page 807 of Hansard for January 30, 1957:
I do want to give the assurance that coupled with the vote of $1 million which I hope the committee will approve we will reiterate the position we have always taken on this matter, that is that the Suez canal shall be free to everyone without discrimination in its use. What form the operative part would take is still a matter of great concern and indeed may not be foreseen at the present time, but the United Nations resolution saying that this waterway shall be open to all users is not only endorsed by Canada but will be endorsed by Canada and insisted upon in so far as we have the ability to do so.
I cannot give a more definite statement than that. We shall do all we can to see, once the canal is open, that that position is maintained. We shall use all the good offices we have at the United Nations-and I think my hon. friend agrees that they are quite extensive because of the high regard for the representative of the Canadian people there- to see that these negotiations and discussions result in the canal being open. Now, whether or not we would say that we would do this or that to achieve that result would depend, of course, on the progress in negotiation. We cannot say at this moment that unless certain conditions are met we shall not go along with this; we are going to do our best to convince all members of the United Nations that this
Supply-External Affairs position should be the ultimate outcome. I, for one, am inclined to think most members here would feel that what can be done will be done by our representatives there and if they are not able to bring it about probably no one would be able to do so.

That is all very well, but the minister has not answered my question so I am going to repeat it. Does the Canadian government believe that the United Nations emergency force should be used in the canal area to ensure the free navigation of the canal? The minister said that the government is in favour of free navigation of the canal. Everyone in Canada agrees with that, but I am not so sure that Egypt does or that Russia does or that a great many other nations agree with it. It is obvious, it seems to me, that we must know something further than that. Here is this United Nations expeditionary force in the Sinai desert. This house was led to believe last fall, I do not know whether or not it was intentional, that Canadian troops were going to take part in the United Nations emergency force in order to bring about free navigation of the canal as well as an armistice between Israel and Egypt. That certainly was the implication contained in the statements of the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I think that is what should be done. I think the United Nations emergency force should carry out that job. Nasser has told us in the last few days that the minute the Israelis withdraw then the United Nations emergency force has to get out of Egypt and that, of course, includes getting out of the Suez canal area. There are two very distinct stands.
I should like to know whether the Canadian government is standing firm on the plan that the United Nations emergency force shall be used in the Suez canal area to ensure that there is free navigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure the Canadian government will stand firm on any pronouncement made by the Prime Minister and by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I would not, however, draw the direct conclusion from what has been said by my hon. friend, that we have made a decision already that the United Nations emergency force ought to be used for the purpose that he has mentioned. In fact, I will go further and say I do not think we have made such a decision, although I quite agree that during the course of the past three months a good many things have been said and done which have affected the whole problem which gave rise to the difficulties we are now considering.
The real purpose of the United Nations force, of course, was to restore a situation in

Supply-External Affairs which peace and stability could be achieved by negotiation. Now, to say at this moment that in three months' time we shall insist on the emergency force staying in the canal area for the purpose of ensuring free navigation in the canal is expecting too much of any government. We would hope that we could achieve the results of free navigation by negotiation. I do not think you enter negotiations with your hands tied too much, and I do not think it would be desirable if we said at this time that only on that basis would we participate in the clearing of the canal. On the other hand, I think we are only-[DOT] to use the Prime Minister's words the other day

dealing in semantics.
Has Nasser given the slightest indication that there will be free navigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; I said that already this morning. He has not, so far as I am aware; but admitting that, I do not think we should sit down and allow things to remain as they are. We have to take some positive action to clean up difficulties which occurred in Egypt and in Israel.

I have two questions in my mind that I wish to put to the minister. First, I must agree with him when he says that our first objective ought to be to get the canal cleared. I think that is understandable. The restoration of navigation in the canal is so important to the well-being and the economies of western Europe and they in turn have to be built up in strength if we are ever going to be able to provide the effective opposition to the communist imperialists that we must present, and I do not think there is anything we can do but to back the minister in his request for this $1 million to get the canal cleared. At the same time, I think we would like to feel that, as we join with the other nations in contributing money to see that the canal is cleared, we are buying one more right to demand that that canal be truly internationalized; that traffic through it be guaranteed to every nation. Furthermore, I think we also ought to make it abundantly clear through the firm attitude that we express that, we are going to see to it eventually that Mr. Nasser pays for the malicious job he did in blocking up that canal.
I never found any more effective way of dealing with a boy who was just a little bit malicious than to make him pay the bill. I do not mean punish him by beating the dickens out of him. That is not my thought. But I saw a lad one time who maliciously broke the windshield of an automobile. His father could very easily have paid the bill; in fact, he did pay it but he said to the boy,


"You are going to have the full cost of this deducted from your allowance over the months until it is fully paid for." That lad never wanted to break another windshield. I think it is exactly the same with Nasser because he is nothing but an overgrown boy and he is silly to boot. My own judgment is that he did this thing maliciously and we ought to make it abundantly clear that he and his country should repay the full cost in due course.
It does seem to me that if we go into this thing with a soft attitude and follow the diffidence that Hammarskjold has used in working with Nasser we will never get anywhere. I would like to believe that when we vote this $1 million and hand it over to the United Nations we ought to say to Mr. Hammarskjold, "You stiffen up on this business now and see to it that ample provision is made, whether through the use of the United Nations emergency force or in some other way, so that the canal zone will be occupied and administered by the United Nations until a perfectly sound agreement has been reached that will continue over the years and guarantee to all nations the right of unimpeded traffic through the canal." That is the first thing.
Then, I think we should also say to Mr. Hammarskjold, "Get it over to Mr. Nasser and his people that they are going to pay this shot and they will have to pay for any further malicious acts of this kind as well." If you stiffen up and do that, Mr. Minister, and see that our representative talks straight turkey to these people we will not hesitate to back you with this $1 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Just to answer-not the last question because I am sure the remarks of my hon. friend will be drawn to the attention of Mr. Hammarskjold-the former question: Before it was agreed to recommend to parliament that this advance should be made we did say to Mr. Hammarskjold what my hon. friend has said-
Thanks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -namely, that we are going to insist, and we will not put this request to parliament unless it is understood-and in doing so our position is quite clear-that this canal must be free.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question but first I would say I do not think there is one of us in this house who would like to see the dictator of Egypt placed in the position of Hitler and Mussolini. Somebody says that the United Nations has given him all the rope possible and he will soon hang himself. We would like to see that day now, but that

is not the question. The point I wish to make is that the United Nations is doing the job of clearing the canal; the work is going on now and it is our duty to pay for it. That is what this $1 million is for.
Has the question of the status of the canal ever been referred to, or judgment passed by, the international court of justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

If not, does the minister not think that this may be an appropriate time, while the canal is being cleared and while there are all these doubts in people's minds as to what the status of the canal shall be, to refer the question to the international court for a ruling in order that the United Nations could then have a clear guidepost lor future action? Obviously, if we are to act as we talk, then the United Nations will have to take some sort of concerted action, or leave it to someone else to take action privately, which is the very thing we are trying to prevent. If the United Nations is going to be called upon or expected to take concerted action for the purpose of making this canal available for all shipping without discrimination, I think it would be of value if it had a clear-cut ruling on what the status is under international law. I should like to hear the minister's opinion on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is no power in the United Nations assembly to compel the reference of a question to the world court. Under those conditions it is unlikely that with the temper of the persons concerned it would go to the world court although it could go by the consent of the nations concerned. Under those conditions I can only say I am quite sure this stratagem to bring about at least a legal opinion about the rights of the countries concerned has no doubt been considered by a great many of the people directly or indirectly involved. As I say, Mr. Chairman, while we here might all agree that that would be a desirable end, at the moment it is not a possible end without the consent of the countries concerned.

I would like to get the answer clear in my mind, Mr. Chairman. The minister says, "without the consent of the countries concerned". In this instance does he refer to Egypt or does he refer to the countries which use the canal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I refer to all countries. You cannot refer a question concerning a country to the world court by compulsion.

Mr. Chairman, I believe it was on Tuesday that the minister said that in making this loan Canada was acting as a
Supply-External Affairs temporary banker for the United Nations. In view of that would the Secretary of State for External Affairs be attempting to replace some of the supermen of Europe to whom the Prime Minister referred in a speech a few weeks ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think, Mr. Chairman, the question was intended as a serious one and the answer ought to be that we are doing our best to bring out of the chaos in the Middle East not only just a cessation of the hostilities which we have already achieved, but a settlement of a great many of the problems which have grown up over a number of years but particularly since 1948. There is lots of evidence to indicate that any action taken requires the good will and the co-operation, either willing or under pressure, of almost every group concerned and that in bringing about that solution we are actuated by only one motive and that is to restore the situation so that trade can be resumed, peace can be more permanently established and, as I always think as Minister of Finance, so that money can be used for the development of trade and the improvement of the standard of living instead of some of the things for which it is now being used.

Mr. Chairman, I understand that the work of clearing the canal has been progressing for at least three weeks or more. Could the Minister of Finance say how those operations have been financed to date? Quite obviously the money must have been paid out to those companies which are doing the salvaging work and wages paid to their personnel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As I said a moment ago, in some cases the salvage companies were doing it on their own or at the cost of the governments concerned. If the salvage companies themselves have not been financing their own operations in the expectation of receiving payment from the United Nations, I can only assume that they are doing the work with some kind of government assistance from their own governments although I have no knowledge that this is so. At any rate through the United Nations there has been no money paid up to the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister made it very clear that at the present time there is no agreement or assurance of any kind with Egypt that they will keep the canal open after it is cleared. I take it from what the minister said that as soon as the canal is cleared it will then be solely under the jurisdiction of the Egyptian government subject to any agreement that may be made through the United Nations. I should like to ask the
884	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs mimsx-r if there has been any discussion so far about this canal and as to any claim that is going to be made for the loss of the revenue from the date the canal was closed until it has been cleared and reopened.
I understand that the average daily revenue at the date the canal was blocked was between $500,000 and $1 million. If that is correct, there is going to be in all probability a large claim made by Egypt against somebody and I would like to know if Canada is then going to be placed in the same position we are in now where we have to pay a part of the cost of clearing the canal and in addition make a contribution toward any claim made by Egypt for loss of revenue during the time when the canal was closed.
The minister said he hoped that, when the canal was cleared, through pressure brought to bear by the United Nations some agreement could be made. Surely the minister remembers how much pressure the United Nations exerted and how hopeless and helpless they were in doing anything about Hungary because Hungary was backed up by Russia. Does he not feel that the United Nations is going to be placed in exactly the same position as far as Egypt is concerned if Egypt refuses to allow the passage of ships of all nations through the canal?
Further, why should not Egypt pay the entire cost of clearing the Suez canal? I do not know the number of ships sunk, but I believe practically all the ships, vessels and barges were sunk by Egypt. If Nasser should fly into a rage again, what is to prevent him from doing exactly the same thing? As far as I am concerned there is nothing that the United Nations can do legally to prevent Nasser operating that canal or blocking the canal again. Once again we are going to place our hopes in the United Nations. I think the minister and the government must realize at this date, which is far too late, that the mistake was in the pressure put on Britain and France by the United Nations, in which Canada played no small part, to withdraw from Port Said. If Britain had been allowed to proceed there the canal would have been protected, would not have been blocked and the United Nations would be in a much better position today than they are.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister indicated that our contribution or loan would be deducted from the assessment we pay to the United Nations fund. Is that to be taken directly from the service the United Nations offers or from the general fund to which we contribute for the operations of the United Nations itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is to be an additional assessment to the annual one of, I think, 3.7 or 3.8 per cent.

May I ask the minister, Mr. Chairman, if he does not consider it reasonable that before we should be asked to vote $1 million to be paid by the people of Canada there should be an attempt which need not take long, and not only an attempt but should it not be decided, that Nasser should give a clear indication of his intention with regard to the future use of this canal? Otherwise does the minister not agree that we are being asked to vote $1 million without any knowledge of whether it is going to be put to useful purposes or thrown away? What is the use of clearing the canal if we find in fact it is not going to be open to ships of all countries who so vitally need it? Why is not an attempt made to obtain a clear and unequivocal statement from Nasser with regard to his intentions concerning the future use of the canal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For the reason I gave a short while ago, Mr. Chairman, that all the advantage at the moment seems to be on the side of clearing the canal pending negotiations for the ultimate use of it rather than doing nothing. I made it quite clear that in the absence of a direct statement by Nasser it is our opinion, and I believe it is the opinion of my hon. friend, that it is better to take three or four months while this work is going on to negotiate this question than to ignore it and have a tremendous cost added on to the various nations that are suffering because of the closing of the canal, and hope that that in itself would be a sufficient reason why in the long run a satisfactory solution might be made. But in any event I must say that it would seem to me that we could not look forward to doing nothing about the canal even if the Egyptian government does at the moment appear to be saying, "We are not going to say now what we will do in three months' time." In effect, that is the situation.

May I just follow that up, because I do not gather from the minister's previous statement that instructions have been issued to the secretary general to obtain a clear statement from Nasser of his intentions. I should not think that that would take three or four months; it should be possible to do that in a matter of days. I do suggest therefore that three or four days should be considered as a reasonable time to devote to obtaining this answer before we and indeed other countries are expected to vote money.
That is not to ignore the problem and the fact that the canal is closed; that is merely to say that we are going to act expeditiously

and tell Mr. Nasser that we are prepared to vote this money, along with the other nations concerned, but before we do so we are entitled to have a clear statement of his intention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I asume that in his negotiations with the Egyptian government, which the secretary general undertook four or five weeks ago, and no doubt in the continuing negotiations which are going on probably every day this question has arisen. However, I do suggest to my hon. friend, who is rather an expert in negotiating on occasion, that one thing you must avoid is having someone at a time when his position may appear to him to be strong or when his feelings are running strong take a position from which he cannot recede at a later time. I should say that that is the first step in diplomacy. If we were to demand an answer from Nasser, an answer involving certain courses of action to be taken, it would seem to me that we might not get very far in achieving a final result.

Can the minister tell us if he knows of any more profitable use to which Mr. Nasser could put the canal than to let ships through? Would he perhaps find it more profitable to grow water lilies in it or to conduct general hydrophonics?

While it is true of course that the "Eisenhower doctrine" is quite apart from the United Nations, nevertheless I should like to ask the minister whether under the pressure which he has pointed out as having to be relied on in dealing with this strange man Nasser he considers that there might not be pressure exerted, either directly or indirectly, through the Eisenhower doctrine to the end that this man will show some common sense?
There are two aspects to the Eisenhower doctrine, one economic and the other military. I repeat what I said at the outset. While the minister may say it is irrelevant, looking at it in the broad, personally it does not seem to me to be irrelevant and I should like to know what the minister thinks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am quite sure that the United States government are as anxious as we are to come to the time in the spring when this work will have been completed and some continuing arrangement made, if not on a permanent at least on a temporary basis, which would permit the free use of the canal pending the outcome of whatever negotiations and discussions are then going on to achieve a permanent political settlement. I think the United States government was the first to say that it would contribute to this fund we are talking about now because
Supply-External Affairs despite the advantages there may be to the Texas oil producers they feel that in the long run and the immediate run there are advantages to the world as a whole in clearing the canal so that oil and many other commodities as well may pass through for western Europe.
I would not want to comment on the recent Eisenhower declaration about Middle East policy because, as I say, that gets into the larger sphere and is included in the larger attitude of restoring and maintaining peace in the Middle East. I would be quite satisfied that the United States administration and the Canadian administration were as one as to the desirability of a final settlement that the canal would be free to the use of all people without restrictions.

Can the minister answer this question on which I am not as well informed as I should be. Is there an indication that the economic aspect of the Eisenhower plan will in the immediate future take as one of its forms a readiness to help in the economic situation? I have been glad to observe recently that some of the oil-producing countries have begun to squawk because they are losing their means of livelihood. I have been wondering for months why the oil-producing countries, some of which live almost entirely on oil, have said so little about the fact that their business was being so greatly hampered and their losses were so great.
I realize that you are dealing with an extraordinary creature in the person of Nasser. I realize that you have to consider the pros and cons and weigh the considerations which might be conclusive to those of us who like to think we are full of common sense but which may not be so compelling in his case. If it is reasonable to believe that Egypt at the present moment is beginning to learn the economic facts of life and that one thing she will have to rely on is assistance from the United States, then it would seem to me reasonable to believe that the Eisenhower doctrine might operate very powerfully.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think it would be unwise to make anything but general comments about political and economic doctrines which are under debate in the United States congress. I join with my hon. friend in the hope that that doctrine and its application, either in the political or economic stage, will be such that it will act, immediately or as soon as possible, with greater pressure to solve the problem now before us. Anything that can help to do that would return dividends, not only in money but in peace for a great many years.

Supply-External Affairs

I know the minister is speaking extemporaneously and is probably not able to choose his words, but I was not very well pleased with his use of the words "levy" and "assessment". It seems to me that it would be wise for the minister to use "assignment" or "allotment". I do not want the idea to get into Hansard that we take the attitude that any group on earth can levy on us or assess us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hasten to agree 100 per cent.

Supplementary to the question I asked a few minutes ago: If I interpret the minister's remarks properly they would indicate that we will be allotted-I am using the word suggested by the hon. member for Lethbridge-a certain sum to be charged the different countries. I am wondering whether all the members of the United Nations have agreed to the plan that they should be allotted a certain figure at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, the resolution has not been debated yet and the attitudes have not been made known.

Has Egypt been asked to pay anything towards the cost of opening the canal? I have not been able to find any reference in the press that such a request has been made. Perhaps the Minister of Finance can give us that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, no one has been asked to pay anything. The only ones who have been asked have been those countries who have been asked to make these temporary advances. The whole question of paying for the costs has yet to be discussed at the United Nations.

Does the minister mean to say that neither Mr. Hammarskjold nor anybody else has even suggested to Egypt that she should pay one cent for clearing the canal although all the damage was done by Egypt? Is that the ridiculous situation in which we are put?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend is very apt at reducing a situation to simple words which do not quite tell the story. It is true that Nasser has not been asked to pay but it is equally true that no one else has been asked to pay, so I agree with his statement put in that form.

The Canadian taxpayer has been asked to pay $1 million. That is what he is being asked this morning. I should like to know why it is that the Canadian taxpayer is paying $1 million and 10 or 15 times as many American taxpayers are being asked to pay only $5 million. Why is it that Canada has to pay a so much larger proportion than the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I went over that on Tuesday and I went over it on Wednesday.
No, you did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh yes. The answer is perfectly simple. First of all, there were a few countries which had dollar assets and for a modest sum of this kind-I use that expression in connection with the total budget-
What's a million?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-and not in connection with the amount involved-they had the exchange available. After consideration of the problem the secretary general decided that he should ask certain countries if they could help immediately by way of advancing a fund of $10 million. At that time the United States offered $5 million which, as I recall it, is more percentagewise than their annual contribution towards the cost of the United Nations. Therefore, taking that yardstick, they offered more than they would otherwise have had to contribute.
When it came to our case we were quite conscious, as I said on Tuesday and Wednesday, that a contribution of one dollar in ten to an interim advance was a greater percentage than we would normally be expected to contribute to any United Nations fund. Our contribution is somewhere below 5 per cent. But because of the fact that we have the dollars, because of the fact that we are a country whose motives are not suspect in any sense of the word in this controversy and because we were in the position that parliament was meeting shortly after it was decided that this would be the best method of interim financing, it was thought that we would have the money available reasonably soon if parliament saw fit to vote it. For that reason we decided after careful consideration on the amount of $1 million knowing nonetheless that it represented a greater portion of the total and a greater proportion with respect to the United States contribution but expecting that the loan will be repaid or, alternatively, that if we are asked later on to make a contribution towards this cost and do so we will be able to recoup the $1 million or a large part of it.
It looks suspiciously' like another case of "what's a million".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not say that.

Perhaps the Minister of Finance can tell us what arrangements, if any, have been made about the payment of tolls for the use of the canal once it is cleared. Are those tolls to be paid to Nasser, to the canal company, to the United Nations or to someone else? What is to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well-

I am not through with my question. Are any negotiations under way at all with regard to the question of the payment of tolls? Is any of the money from tolls to be used to repay the cost of clearing the canal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There are no negotiations publicly at the moment. There are a good many discussions going on at the United Nations as to the outcome of the use of the canal. One method suggested for repaying this money is to increase the tolls and make a charge of some kind on the tolls which would be collected and remitted to the United Nations in repayment of this sum of money. But, as I have indicated this morning, there has been no decision made because the whole question of financing has not yet been discussed by the United Nations.
What about my question as to the authority to which the tolls are to be paid? Has that been decided?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That has not been decided. It will be decided along with the other questions when the United Nations comes to the resolution as to what will be done when the canal is cleared and made available for shipping.

It seems to me that the minister has certainly given us every assurance that our representatives at the United Nations will try to establish that we do get the money repaid. It also seems to me that the greatest beneficiary from the use of the canal is the United Kingdom. Having felt as we have in the past about this whole conflict, I would say that under the circumstances it is very desirable that we see to it that the $1 million is voted very shortly.

I want to know if I understood the minister correctly a few minutes ago when I thought he said that in paying over the money we would indicate that it was being done on the condition that the canal must be free for all. Did I understand the minister correctly?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. I answered that in a different form the other day when replying to the hon. member for Winnipeg North. I said we could not impose sanctions on the use of the $1 million. Once we give it to the secretary general it will be for the purpose of clearing the canal. We are going to do that but I said at the same time that we would accompany the cheque with a restatement of our support for the resolution of the United Nations calling upon the powers concerned to make the canal free and that we would continue to insist in negotiations at the United
Supply-External Affairs Nations that that be the ultimate outcome of the negotiations.

Can the minister say whether or not Russia has stated that she will not pay any part of the cost of clearing the canal? I did see where she had stated that in her opinion Britain and France should pay the whole cost. I believe she has also stated she will not pay any part.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That was a statement attributed to one of the representatives of Russia at the United Nations but in connection with a debate which has not yet arisen there, and one is hopeful that there may be a change, although I am not going to suggest that there will be.

What consideration has been given to the suggestion that it is possible to construct another canal not on Egyptian territory? I am not in a position to know whether or not such a course is feasible but we have seen reports to that effect. If no one is going to put this man Nasser in his place it might be a good idea for investigations to be made as to the possibility of an alternative canal. It does seem to me that action along that line is much more likely to get reasonable action out of Nasser than for the freedom-loving nations like Canada to go on hoping that Nasser is going to be fair.
That is all we are doing today. I realize that the minister cannot take any other stand. He cannot say anything else because it is perfectly obvious that that is what Canada is doing as well as the United States, namely just hoping that Nasser is going to do what they want him to do. Would it not strengthen our hand a great deal if at least real steps were taken to find out whether or not it is possible to construct an alternative canal? Certainly if that can be done, Mr. Nasser and his Suez canal will be high and dry and we probably would not have much more trouble from him. Just what is the picture with regard to that possibility?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The original canal, of course, was a private venture backed by certain governments for the purpose of profit, and I am satisfied that in the intervening years it has become quite profitable. This would only mean that there would be a possibility of competition from others who would feel that they might make a profit too. It seems to me that this is a case where these matters would probably be present in the mind of Colonel Nasser. But in any event I think that every possible alternative to future trouble over the canal ought to be explored. If any one were in a position seriously to advocate a canal in another position or an alternative method of transportation such as

Ways and Means
the Israelis are attempting and are carrying out with some success, I am told, that would be one more economic reason why, in the course of these negotiations, we might come out with a reasonably good settlement.

After listening to this debate for two full days now or nearly that much, the muddied water so far as I am personally concerned is becoming clearer every minute, and I am becoming more in favour of passing this vote and granting this money to the United Nations. I want to make myself clear on this position. At the time that Great Britain and France went into this canal zone, there is no doubt at all in my mind that the United States let them down for political expediency and that at that particular time Our Canadian representative played no small part in letting them down. They sold Mr. Eden down the river. There is no doubt about that. For that mistake which we made, if for no other reason, we should pay the piper. This is one way of paying him. We should pay this amount whether we get the money back or whether we do not. I have not much faith in ever getting it back. These loans or investments or whatever you call them made in this sort of way are generally give-away programs. But if we made a mistake-and there is no doubt that our officials did so at that time-let us pay the piper.
