speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 9, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.

He said: The purpose of Bill No. 9 is to extend for another five years certain vital sections of the Canadian Wheat Board Act which expire at the end of this crop year, that is on July 31 next. These sections have the effect of maintaining the wheat board as the sole marketing agency for western wheat, oats and barley.
The Canadian wheat board is in its 14th year of operation as the sole agency for the marketing of wheat produced in western Canada. During that time it has encountered nearly every conceivable combination of production and international trading conditions. There have been rusted, wet and frozen crops; there have been large and small crops; there have been periods of shortage when special measures were necessary to allocate supplies; more recently there have been unprecedentedly large crops at a time of intense international competition.
The board has met and dealt with these problems and today has more widespread support amongst producers and producers' organizations than ever before. This widespread support is, I think the house will agree, a tribute to the soundness of the present wheat board system of marketing and to the devoted and skilful work of the members of the board, in particular of course the work of George Mclvor, who has been a member of the board almost since its inception and who has been its chief commissioner since 1937.
The producers of western Canada understand thoroughly what the board is and how it operates today. That is why they give it such wholehearted support. I regret to say that there is less understanding in certain other quarters, and if the house will bear with me I should like to give a brief review of the origins and purposes of the present system of marketing.
The present system of wheat board marketing is an outgrowth of the pooling system which got under way in the early 1920's. All members from the prairies are familiar with the establishment of the Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta wheat pools. The basic idea was that members of the pools should deliver their grain to the pool and receive an initial price at the time of delivery, and the balance of the sales price, less expenses, when all grain had been sold. A central selling agency was established to co-ordinate the selling activities of the three provincial pools. The pools operated on this basis throughout the 1920's with considerable success and without any intervention or help from governments. Unfortunately, however, they became victims of the great depression. Although the initial prices for deliveries from the huge 1928 wheat crop, and deliveries from the 1929 crop, had been fixed at what seemed
Canadian Wheat Board Act reasonably conservative levels, the market collapse of the early 1930's prevented them from realizing enough from sales to cover these initial advances, plus expenses. The provincial governments first came to the rescue by guaranteeing the advances made by the chartered banks. So great was the debacle, however, that in the fall of 1930 the federal government had to provide additional guarantees to the banks.
At the same time, the government of Canada appointed John I. McFarland as manager of the pools' central selling agency. Mr. McFarland was instructed to stabilize the market, and this he did by buying both cash grain and futures on the open market for government account. Between November 30, 1930 and December 2, 1935, the central selling agency, which became divorced from the wheat pools and became instead the stabilization agency for the Canadian government, increased its holdings of wheat from 37 million bushels to 205 million bushels. Meanwhile the provincial pools operated on a small scale. This was the situation when the Canadian wheat board came into existence in 1935. It took over the wheat accumulated during the stabilization operations of the previous five years, and it stood ready to take wheat from producers at an initial price, and to return the proceeds of sale, less expenses, to the producers.
Hon. members will note that the Canadian wheat board at this stage was not the sole marketing agency for wheat. It stood ready to take delivery from producers, at a stated initial price, but producers could, if they wished, sell on the open market. In other words, it was at this time a board operating a voluntary pool. And so it continued to be until September 1943. While on the voluntary basis, the activities of the board fluctuated widely and rapidly. When the open market was above the initial prices, producers delivered relatively small quantities to the board. When the open market was below the initial price, producers delivered practically all their wheat to the board. From the point of view of a successful marketing operation by the board, this was a most unsatisfactory position. In a sense it was a sort of "heads I win, tails you lose" proposition. And as events were to prove, the producers themselves preferred a different system.
During the period of the voluntary pool the wheat board suffered one major loss arising out of the marketing of the 1938 crop, amounting to over $60 million. There were one or two other minor losses, but with these exceptions the boards not only sold at high enough prices to cover its initial advances and expenses, but also to make a further payment

Canadian Wheat Board Act to producers who had delivered wheat to the board. In September 1943 the wheat board became the sole marketing agency for wheat produced in the prairie region. Acting under authority of the War Measures Act, the government discontinued trading in wheat futures at Winnipeg. Special arrangements were made for the sale of wheat under mutual aid, and to meet the requirements of subsidized domestic purchasers. And the initial price was raised from 90 cents to $1.25.
This was the turning point in the recent history of wheat board operations. In September 1943 the present system, which enjoys such widespread support, came into effect. At the end of the war, of course, it was necessary for parliament, by the enactment of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, to put the system on a peacetime basis rather than on the basis of the War Measures Act, but otherwise the essentials were preserved. It is worthy of note that, since the board became the sole marketing agency, it has always been fully solvent and has always been able to make payments to its producers in addition to the initial payment. So popular did the present system prove to be that strong representations were made to extend it to oats and barley, which was done, effective as from August 1, 1949. Because of the constitutional position applying to grains like oats and barley, which are very largely consumed within the province of their production, the government insisted upon provincial legislation in each of the three prairie provinces to support the wheat board as the sole marketing agency.
That is the history. Now let me describe the system as it operates today. In effect, the wheat board operates a pool for the benefit of all producers, with the advantage of government support in its financing. The government, on recommendation of the board, fixes initial prices for deliveries during the crop year at what appear to be reasonable levels, taking into account prospects of sale. The board pays the producer initial advances on grain delivered to the pool by borrowing money from the banks, under government guarantee. The board sells the wheat and, after paying all expenses, returns the proceeds of sale to the producer in the form of further payments.
The board is a producers' board and even the salaries of board members are paid by the producers. The money involved is wholly money belonging to the producers, even though the board's bank borrowings are guaranteed by the government.
The board is strictly a marketing organization. It has no other functions whatever. Its aim is to market as much grain as possible, at

as high prices as possible, to keep its expense to a minimum, and to provide as high a degree of equity in delivery opportunities amongst producers as can be achieved within the limits of its overriding duty of selling grain.
In my opinion, the board has done a magnificent job in carrying out these functions and in attaining these objectives. And the secret of its success lies in the fact that it has not allowed its energies to be diverted in other directions.
That is the main reason why, on every and all occasions, the board, strongly supported by the government, has resisted efforts to put the board into the money-lending business by making advances to producers against grain stored on farms. That is not the business of the wheat board and should not be its business. To put the wheat board into the business of making farm advances is the surest way I know of playing into the hands of those who would like to wreck the board as an effective marketing agency for the producer.
Hon. members may wonder why I have tried to explain in detail the nature of the wheat board and the manner in which it functions. Those hon. members who represent prairie constituencies and many other hon. members require no such detailed explanation. Strangely enough, many people living in other parts of Canada who write and talk about the marketing of wheat obviously do not understand the detail of present methods of marketing Canadian wheat. It is to them that my explanation is directed.
A case in point is the Gordon commission which, after an extensive investigation, has produced a preliminary report that is obviously based on incorrect understanding of present marketing methods. In paragraph 5 of the section on wheat the following section appears:
Under the present system the Canadian wheat board announces shortly before the harvest each year the initial or minimum prices which will be paid for the crop which is about to be harvested. These minimum prices, which vary depending upon the grade, apply to the full amount of the crop . . .
That statement, of course, is a complete misconception. The government authorizes the board to fix an initial price for such wheat as may be delivered to the board within the next crop year, and guarantees the banks against loss through payment of the initial price, but the government does not guarantee payment to the farmer of any price for wheat which is not actually delivered to the board within the crop year.
It will be obvious to the hon. members from the prairies that the board cannot

possibly form an accurate estimate of the amount of grain which can be delivered to the board in any future crop year. Conditions in the export market change from month to month to an extent that can greatly change export prospects for better or for worse.
No reasonable man would ask the board to undertake the quite impossible task of fixing delivery quotas for individual producers on the basis of past records of acreage and yield. As a matter of fact, there are no available records which would be of any help to the board for such a purpose. Furthermore, it is the farmers' money that the Gordon commission would pay out on the basis of such an export forecast and on delivery quotas for individual producers fixed as recommended by the Gordon commission. Before taking any steps toward implementing the recommendations of the Gordon commission, the government would require almost unanimous support from the producers' marketing organizations. 1 feel sure that that support will not be forthcoming.
If any hon. member wishes to be recorded in support of the recommendations of the Gordon commission I hope that he will rise in his place and state his position clearly and unequivoc ally.
The underlying theme of the Gordon report on wheat is "restriction". The report returns time and again to the theme that the producer must be confronted with a limitation under which he will make whatever adjustments he can. This conception is directly opposed to the present government policy, which is to establish fair initial prices, provide the largest possible delivery opportunity for producers and to assist by paying carrying charges on abnormal surplus stocks of wheat until markets can be found.
The Gordon commission recommendations appear to be based upon the assumption that there is likely to be a continuing surplus problem. I do not share that view and I think it would be a great mistake to base our policies on such an assumption.
I have said many times, and I say it again, that the only reason that any substantial surplus of wheat remained on farms at the end of the last crop year, and is likely to remain on farms at the end of the current crop year, is the remarkable series of bumper crops. Had crops been average, or even moderately above average, in recent years not a bushel of grain would be on farms today other than grain that the farmer himself preferred to hold. But crops have not been just above average but of unprecedented proportions in recent years.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
In fact, farmers have marketed very large quantities of grain every year. Our exports on the whole have been at satisfactory levels. Last crop year, for example, they were well above all except a very few preceding years and domestic consumption is now, of course, more substantial than it has even been. This crop year our exports are considerably higher to date than they were in the same period during the last crop year.
The outlook is not gloomy. The wheat board has a difficult task but it has demonstrated that it knows how to handle its task. It will at all times receive the full support of the government.
I have no hesitation in recommending an extension of the present system of wheat board marketing for a period of five years.

The events of the last few months have added emphasis to the demand of last year that there should be incorporated in this act a permanent provision for cash advances in order to assure western farmers of a reasonable opportunity to meet their initial costs and expenditures. The minister says that anyone who would advocate that policy would be a participant in contributing to the destruction of the board. Well, Mr. Speaker, if that be so then the western farm organizations and the pools themselves must be in that category. Certainly farmers in general who support the wheat board marketing system are almost universally in support of incorporating a provision for cash advances in the act which I believe is necessary having regard to the uncertainty of marketing arid storage difficulties.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
When that course was advocated last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said that he had communicated with the members of the wheat board and they had given him to understand that if a system of cash advances was brought into effect they would resign. I asked for the production of the correspondence to that effect and also a summary of the conversations which allegedly had taken place. The answer given in reply to that request was that there were no records and there was no correspondence. The hon. gentleman reviewed some of the wheat board's transactions and having done that I may be pardoned for also filling in, in what he called a review of the origins and purposes of the wheat board, certain things to which he did not make reference.
I think it is appropriate to review the history of this board since 1935. It was in 1935 that the late R. B. Bennett, the then prime minister, introduced the Wheat Board Act in the House of Commons. It was his desire and purpose that it should be a compulsory board much in keeping with the present situation in so far as the compulsory features are concerned. However, the Liberal opposition of that day opposed him and on July 1, 1935 after a series of discussions between members of the government and the opposition it was finally agreed that the only way in which the legislation could find itself on the statute books would be by having the voluntary feature incorporated and not the compulsory feature.

Secondly, the United States sells wheat for payment in the currency of the buyer. In other words, this is a form of foreign aid, rather than a method of sale.
Thirdly, the United States attempts to trade its wheat against strategic materials. I do not think it is unfair to say, from the evidence available, that the emphasis is more on disposing of wheat than on securing supplies of strategic materials. Fourthly, the United States offers wheat without payment to countries which are in dire need, because of some calamity. In principle, of course, there can be no objection to such gifts, provided that they are not used to destroy commercial markets, which would otherwise have been available.
Then the minister continued:
As I said, I do not think that the United States intends to harm Canada by any of its policies.
Those are sweet words from one usually given to strong expression.
Yet there can be no doubt that, whatever the intention, the methods used by the United States to dispose of its wheat surpluses have been harmful, not only to Canada, but to the wheat situation in general.
And again:
When the members of the United States cabinet were in Ottawa in September-
That was September 1955.
-to meet members of the Canadian cabinet, I put the Canadian point of view before our American friends more strongly than ever before.
Well they did not listen even then. What did he say, what were the strong words that were used? The government of this country has been blaming the United States for the loss of markets, and the wheat board has been doing the same. Mr. Mclvor, chairman of the wheat board, said on July 4, 1956, that United States policy was the main reason for loss of wheat markets by Canada. He said markets were lost for reasons beyond our control. He then went on to say that they were lost because the United States was engaging in a system that was not justifiable.
Well, Mr. Speaker, they did not find out how serious it was until October, 1956. They always contended that the Americans were acting in an injudicious way but that what they were doing might be justified. It was only in October, 1956, that they found out. We have these wheat merchants and trade commissioners all over the world and yet they did not find out until then or a few
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
weeks before that the United States was engaged in a most improper practice whereby in the disposal of farm produce the nation that received the benefit of these give-away terms or reduced prices undertook to buy future requirements from the United States. In other words, these gifts, these fire sales, in effect carried with them a gobbling up of wheat markets in the future which no one can justify under the terms of the agreement on tariffs and trade.
Mr. Victor Mackie, writing in the Winnipeg Free Press, had this to say on October 8, 1956:
Only this summer Canadian officials began to become aware of the important part this provision in the American surplus disposal program was playing in United States disposal of its produce. One report published in a Toronto financial paper in a Washington dispatch states that it was not until the Canadian-U.S. meeting of officials in Winnipeg August 28 that the Canadian government discovered the "tied" sales, which had been standard U.S. operating procedure in its disposal program.
It had continued for several years. The article goes on to say that Canada's government has moved in the diplomatic field to put a stop to the tied deals for the future and has sent a formal note of protest.
Where were they, Mr. Speaker, during the two years? Why did they not find this out? We were losing important markets. The United States was concealing nothing. It gave away wheat and other agricultural products either at lower prices or almost as a gift but always tied to the undertaking on the part of the receiving country that that country would continue to purchase further wheat or other agricultural products. I could quote from various editorials in other western newspapers. The Winnipeg Free Press, the Regina Leader-Post, the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix and other newspapers that support the government found it difficult to understand why the government was blind for two long years as to what was going on while we were losing our markets.
To say we have increased our exports of wheat does not meet the question at all. We have increased our exports and so have other countries. The United States has increased its exports the greatest of all and has taken over our place and forced us into a secondary position in this regard. We tried to find out what the government had done. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said that he had spoken in strong terms to them. What was said? Whatever was said has not brought about any change. Why can parliament not find out? On the 24th of January, as found at page 589 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce what

had been done, what was the nature of the protest, and in reply he said:
The two governments have appointed a continuing committee of senior civil servants of both governments to deal with these matters. The committee meets from time to time. I think the last meeting was some two or three weeks ago. Protests are filed through that committee, and sometimes remedial action is taken.
There has been no remedial action in connection with wheat that can be seen by any eyes anywhere in the world. He goes to say:
Protests, I may say, are sometimes filed in both directions. In any event we find that committee has been useful as a means of conveying our protests, and has had some effect in discouraging certain policies to which we in Canada take strong objection. There is nothing to table. We do not file our protests in writing; we file them through the committee.
Then I asked the minister whether he would tell us what had been done and what was the nature of the protest, and this was his answer:
Mr. Speaker, to discuss in parliament the subject matters that are dealt with by the committee would be to destroy the usefulness of the committee.
I would have destroyed the effectiveness of the alleged objections being raised. That, Hr. Speaker, is what it would have done. Parliament? Why tell parliament anything? They are talking the thing over in such strong words that parliament dare not hear them.The minister goes on to say:
I do not know that it is particularly in the public interest to discuss the kind of transactions we object to. Certain transactions we do object to; but to single them out and discuss them on the floor of the house would, as I say, seriously prejudice the future of the continuing committee.
In other words, parliament which set up the wheat board, parliament which is interrested in the trade of this country, parliament which desires to know what is being done in order to prevent the loss of markets by improper procedures on the part of the United States, is to be denied information. Finally, Mr. Speaker, after I had raised that point and said how unfair it was the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said:
If the hon. gentleman reads what was being talked about before he rose and reads his own remarks, he will find how inappropriate they are to what has been the subject of discussion.
My remarks were these:
. . . does the Prime Minister not believe that parliament has a right to hear?
Is there anything inappropriate in that?
Is everything to be hidden under the new policy or the continuation of the old one that is being followed ... by the government of concealing all information that it does not want parliament or the people to have?
Sir, we have lost these markets for the future. We have lost them because the United
Canadian Wheat Board Act States has adopted a policy of tying in future deliveries and promises of future deliveries with the present-day give-away and fire sale policy. Surely parliament is entitled to ascertain how strong these protests are or whether in this regard Canada's economic future in agriculture is to be sacrificed to the desire of the government to conceal the pusillanimity of its protests. Are they afraid to speak out? The United States is not. We are joined together. We supply the United States with a major portion of its needs to forge the shield of freedom. We are a have country and they are becoming a have-not country.
Surely a protest should be made to the government of the United States that could be heard, not one of these listless, silent protests that are conveyed through a group of civil servants, senior though they may be, whose protests dare not come to the light of day through parliament which created the wheat board. The Canadian people are denied information on a matter upon which they are entitled to information.
We say, sir, that in the last several years the Department of Trade and Commerce has not exercised that degree of diligence in the securing of markets that it should have. We are treated regularly to optimistic statements, and while Canada's parliament receives optimistic statements the United States of America gobbles up future wheat markets and denies us in Canada any opportunity in the future to deal competitively with the United States of America.
I come now to one other matter, the general position of the farmer, particularly with regard to agricultural prices, and the difficulty the farmer finds himself in today by reason of the fact that he is caught in a squeeze between falling farm prices and rising costs. This was dealt with during the last few days by the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. I refer to an editorial in the Western Producer, summarizing the situation, on January 17. Mr. Wesson was dealing with the export of Canadian wheat and flour, and he said this:
The improvement in exports was reflected during part of the year in good delivery opportunities at country elevators throughout the west.
Then I leave out a few lines, not that they are not material, and continue:
These additional marketings last year have given farmers a higher cash income for 1956 than they enjoyed in 1955.
That is a higher cash income. In fact they are receiving year by year a lower net income. Then he goes on to say this:
But even on the basis of these good sales many farmers did not break even on the year's operations.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
He is speaking in particular of the wheat farmer.
The continued high cost of things needed to operate a farm and to maintain the farm family was putting the farmer in an impossible position. The price he received for his grain and other agricultural products was too low to keep the average farmer out of debt.
Then he went on to point out this:
The improvement in income in 1956 will not bridge the gap between costs and prices as shown in 1955 figures. The result is that many farmers are dipping into reserves to keep going while other farmers are accumulating debts which will be extremely difficult to pay at present prices.
Then he said the future is bright for wheat, and ended in this way:
The disparity between costs and prices will in all probability continue to have a serious effect on farm people throughout the coming year . . . The continued high cost of things needed to operate a farm and to maintain the farm family is putting the farmer in an impossible position.
That is something we have been bringing to the attention of the house over and over again in recent years. That was one of the reasons we have advocated-and I again advocate it-in view of the loss of our wheat markets through the actions to which I have referred, that in the interests of maintaining and extending a continued increase in our wheat marketing we should convene in Canada at the earliest possible date a British commonwealth trade conference in order to ascertain in consultation, as I expect can be achieved, whether or not we shall be able to secure a larger share of the wheat marketing within the commonwealth.
What about India? Under this scheme she has entered into an agreement with the United States to take $400 million worth of wheat and other farm products, a practical giveaway. Surely if a commonwealth conference were convened such things would not be taking place. In any event, the condition would be alleviated and a larger share of the wheat market would be made available. Why not call the conference? What harm can there be in doing so? If anyone argues with me that nothing can be achieved, then I ask why it is that we send trade commissioners all over the world. Let us convene such a conference and endeavour to secure for the future some of the markets for our wheat which are being lost.
We said the same thing in 1928 and 1929, namely that the markets for wheat were being lost. If you read the speech from the throne in 1929 and 1930 you will find that the Governor General uttered words to the effect that all was well, that we had on hand and unsold more wheat than ever before. We lost our markets then as we are losing them today. We are not only losing our markets for today, but by improper practices that

are countenanced by this government through its failure adequately to object, we are losing our markets for the future.
This brings to mind a further suggestion that I place before the government in connection with agriculture in general, and wheat and other farm products in particular. Now that the Supreme Court of Canada has given its judgment on the jurisdiction of the dominion parliament and the provincial legislatures in connection with agricultural boards and the like, I suggest that there should be convened a conference of dominion and provincial representatives on agriculture and also representatives of the various agricultural bodies in this country, to the end that in a community of discussion we may be able to determine a course of marketing for wheat and other farm products, and also assure that agriculture shall not continue in its present position of being caught in a squeeze between rising costs and falling farm prices.
These are but one or two suggestions. There are others I could have made, but at the moment I will rest at this point and merely say this in summary. We support the legislation continuing the wheat board. It is natural that we should do so, for we gave it birth and we have given it support throughout the years. In the second place, I suggest that the wheat board should operate as an independent body for the producers, and in no way to carry out government policy under the direction of the government to the detriment of the farmer. In the third place I suggest that in order to meet the serious challenge to our agricultural markets, and in particular our wheat markets of which I am speaking at the moment, parliament has the right to know what this government is doing. Is it whispering to the United States?
It is playing golf.

When you look at the situation in Europe today you find that Britain for the first time in all her history has commenced to look to the continent of Europe for a free-trade area. Britain is only held back by her desire not to do any harm to the agricultural products which she purchases today from various parts of the commonwealth.
What is the government doing in that regard? What will be the result if this free trade area is opened? What loss will be suffered by Canadians, and in particular by the wheat farmers? What is Canada doing in regard to this innovation in international trade on the continent of Europe to assure that her markets for wheat will not be lost there, and what is she doing in order to assure the continuance and maintenance of the British market?
Then, sir, one final suggestion is the convening now in Ottawa of representatives of the dominion and provincial departments of agriculture and of farm bodies generally. Realizing the distribution of powers between dominion and provincial governments and the limitations on the exercise of federal and provincial jurisdictions, we should act in order to do something on behalf not only of the wheat farmers but of farmers generally in all parts of Canada.

We in this group, Mr. Speaker, will vote for second reading of the bill. We do so because we believe in an orderly system for the marketing of wheat and other grains. I listened very carefully to the remarks made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon. When he says that the western producers almost unanimously support the wheat board, he is correct. When he says that the producers of western Canada believe the present personnel of the Canadian wheat board have done a very good job, considering all the circumstances, he is correct.
But I was disappointed that the minister did not demonstrate his own belief and the
Canadian Wheat Board Act belief of the government in the good job the Canadian wheat board has been doing under these circumstances by proposing to parliament that the Canadian Wheat Board Act be made permanent legislation. Apparently the government is converted to the principle of the wheat board on a temporary basis. The minister says we are asking parliament now to consider giving the wheat board a further life of five years. We have heard a lot of talk this afternoon about a great many of the problems that face producers in the marketing of grain, but I have heard few suggestions as to what should be done to help farmers; what should be done now to put more money into the pockets of the farmers; what should be done now to see that within the next few months farmers are able to sell more grain.
We believe in the wheat board system of marketing grain. We in this group believe in it because we believe it will be more and more demonstrated that it is necessary for a government to involve itself to an even greater extent in the marketing of such commodities produced in this country. We believe in it because we believe there is an important field in this country to be occupied by public ownership and by public planning. The wheat board is part and parcel of the principles and beliefs of the members of this group. So we say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that if he himself were in fact completely sold on the principle of orderly marketing under the Canadian wheat board, he would not be proposing to parliament at this time a bill to extend the life of the Canadian wheat board another five years, but he would be presenting to parliament a bill to make the wheat board a permanent part of the economy of this country. In addition, he would be proposing that the wheat board handle oats and barley outside the Winnipeg grain exchange, and would prepare an amendment to the present act so the wheat board would be empowered as the sole marketing agency for rye and flax.
The minister has divided himself and his beliefs into two compartments. Part of the minister's belief is in the Canadian wheat board, that is true; the other part of his belief is a belief in the Winnipeg grain exchange, keeping their doors open and allowing the future market to operate to the detriment of the producers.
Producers well know just how the futures market has operated in recent months to their detriment. A year ago last fall when the farmers were selling flax they were getting just over $2 a bushel. When they decided in the spring to buy some seed to

Canadian Wheat Board Act sow flax they found the price was up to $4 or $4.25. When they marketed their flax through the Winnipeg grain exchange, through the speculative market, the price was low. In the spring when they went into the market to buy flax, they found the price was high. I suggest that right now the government, if it wants the approval of he Canadian wheat and grain producers, should introduce an amendment giving the exclusive marketing of oats, flax, barley and rye to the wheat board. Then they would close the grain exchange and, in effect, put a padlock on gambling and throw away the key.
The minister is not interested in supporting a system of orderly marketing to that extent. We believe, too, there should be a system of cash advances. We supported that idea last year and we support it now. I suggest that at this moment, in this crop year, farmers are very much in need of such a system of cash advances.
Then the minister took this opportunity to condemn the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. This commission was a child of the government, but the minister has condemned its report by a very sweeping statement to the effect that certain sections of the report are completely impracticable. I do not agree with one section at all, but perhaps for different reasons from the minister. We in this group would not be satisfied with the proposal of the royal commission that the wheat board make a guess as to the amount of wheat it would be able to accept, and then provide for an initial price based on that quantity. If marketing conditions were not good and the amount of grain the wheat board could export was not large, then the farmers' income would be very low. A further item that is not mentioned is what would happen if the wheat board were able to take more grain than they judged they would be able to accept. Would they take it at a guaranteed price or at a lower price? I think the whole section of the royal commission report dealing with agriculture generally is very inadequate and, to make a general statement, the implementation of that report would not meet the needs of the farmers in this country.
We would like to see the principles of the Canadian wheat board extended. We would like to see the government take action to improve the sales and exports of Canadian grain. A year ago the minister made a very optimistic statement to this house as to the future of wheat exports. Today he did not make any optimistic forecasts. He did not say we would be marketing, in this crop year, a much larger quantity than we did

last year, or exporting a much larger quantity. All he said was that the outlook was not gloomy and went on to say that the wheat board has a difficult task.
The other day, in making a speech outside of this house, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as reported in the Globe and Mail on January 24, had this to say on this point:
I would mislead you, however, if I did not add that, in order to produce satisfactory results, the wheat board and all others concerned, will have to work harder than ever to sell our grain in overseas countries. Competition shows no signs whatever of abating, and the high current level of ocean freights constitutes a new and formidable problem.
We all know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce looks on everything in a very optimistic way, but in this instance he has changed. He is not painting an optimistic picture. I can only conclude that the Minister of Trade and Commerce himself feels that the near future for the marketing of wheat is very uncertain indeed. I saw a report by the Alberta wheat pool, published in the Alberta Wheat Pool Budget of January 11, which states that the reports received on future sales of wheat are discouraging. The Alberta Wheat Pool Budget goes on to say it does not appear certain at this time whether or not Canada will export during the present crop year even as much wheat as we exported last year.
Last year our exports of wheat increased considerably over the year before. In studying why we were able to sell 309 million bushels of wheat in the face of very severe competition from the United States I found there were three main reasons. The first was that there was a poor European crop. They had a very bad winter in Europe a year ago, so that sales to Europe from Canada were increased. The Argentine experienced a very poor crop, and for that reason competition from the Argentine was lessened. Probably the main reason was that last year there were very substantial quantities of wheat purchased from Canada by certain Soviet bloc countries. These exports to countries in the Soviet bloc amounted to a total of some 45 million bushels.
The picture now seems to be changing. The Argentine crop, which has just been taken off, is estimated to be something of the order of 253 million bushels as compared with 193 million bushels last year. Australia has been successful in increasing her exports from 90.6 million bushels a year ago to 130 million bushels in the most recent crop year. In this situation we see that the wheat board is experiencing some difficulty in selling and exporting Canadian wheat, even

Canadian Wheat Board Act
though in the current crop year the record, compared with the same period last year, has been better.
Last year, in the period from August to November, our exports were some 28 million bushels fewer than they have been in the same period this year. In that same period this year we exported 106 million bushels. The United States exported 150 million bushels, or 44 million bushels more than Canada was able to export. The Canadian Wheat Review for December, 1956, shows that for the first time since 1951, in the period from August to November, United States sales of wheat, or exports of wheat, exceeded those of Canada.

speechtext: Don't use the word "sales".

Almost every other country in the world has long since decided that the people who farm and produce food are entitled to an equitable living on a par with people engaged in other occupations. The United States is now paying a support price of $2 a bushel, Japan $2.59 a bushel, France $2.64 a bushel, Turkey $2.91 a bushel, Norway $3.43 a bushel, Switzerland $4.03 and so on. Countries across the world have decided that adequate support prices should be implemented but this government, believing as it does in the free market system to the extent it can get away with it, continues to return to the farmer only the number of dollar bills it can obtain on the world markets.
The United States government is very directly engaged in the marketing of the grain of that country. The Republican government elected in 1952 said it was determined to get out of the wheat business, and its policy was to withdraw any government control of agricultural commodities. Today the Republican administration of the United States is more deeply involved in the marketing of agricultural commodities than any previous Democratic government had been. The United States are grabbing the wheat markets of the world.
Much has been said in criticism of the policies of the United States government in this regard. I have some information concerning the large quantities of wheat the United States government has been able to dispose of under its various policies. I doubt if many hon. members realize the large degree to which the United States has corralled the present wheat markets of the world. The information I have obtained indicates that under title I of public law 480 the United States since 1954 has contracted for the sale of 2,073 million bushels of wheat. Under section 402 of public law 665 concerning the acceptance of defence material the United States has sold $393 million worth of wheat. Under title 2 of public law 480, which is the gift section involving the provision of food in the event of famine, approximately 40 million bushels of wheat have been exported. All in all under these policies the United States as I understand it has contracted and agreed to the sale of some 2,200 million or 2,300 million bushels of wheat.
I suggest that even if the government sent the entire cabinet to Washington to protest the actions of the United States under these policies nothing could be accomplished because the damage has already been done. Even if the United States were asked to break its contractual obligations with importing countries the answer of that country is

bound to be in the negative. There is no hope for us this way. We can merely protest, saying we do not like it. I suggest we can shout as loud as possible and make as much noise as we like, but it will probably not result in the sale of an additional bushel of wheat.
The United States has corralled some of Canada's best markets. The United States has entered the Brazilian market, and has a three-year contract for the sale of $200 million worth of wheat to India. The Indian market is in large part already lost to Canada. Last year we were able to develop an additional market in iron curtain countries. Last year during the first nine months we sold to Poland, Russia and Czechoslovakia a total of $60.4 million of products, mainly wheat. During the same period we imported from those countries a mere $6.1 million worth of goods. I am now wondering if the difference between the export and import figures explains why these countries have not so far this year purchased any wheat from Canada. Certainly it will be impossible for Canada to continue selling to these countries ten times as much as we are prepared to import from them.
It is for this reason that hon. members of this group say the time has come for this government to adopt new policies governing the sale of wheat and other commodities. We suggest once again as we have so often suggested in the past that the government should be prepared to accept local currency from any country that might want to buy our wheat. We should agree not to turn the local currency into dollars but to block it in that country and be prepared to use it in the future for the purchase of goods produced in that country, or for investment in the countries which have purchased our wheat.
We think that is a sensible policy. We think that is a policy which will increase our sales. We think that is a policy which will return us something for the wheat which we have to sell. We suggest further that it is not good enough to sell wheat to countries which may wish to buy it from us on a contractual basis. We suggest that we should be prepared to say to Russia, Czechoslovakia and Poland, "If you are prepared to buy our wheat we will agree to purchase substantial quantities of the goods you produce so you can keep on being a good market for our products." I am afraid that if we continue to say to the nations of the world, "We will sell only if you pay hard money" we will continue to experience great difficulty in the selling of our wheat. The danger is that the United States may grab more and more of the markets we have enjoyed.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
To sum up, I suggest that there are at least six practical things the government could do now, things that are not just talk, not just window dressing, but acts by the government which would benefit the agricultural producers in Canada.
First, I suggest that the government should extend the operations of the wheat board to cover the marketing of oats, barley, flax and rye in their entirety, and thus bring about the final closing of the Winnipeg grain exchange.
Second, I suggest that the government should extend the principle of paying storage on grain, such storage to be paid on all wheat held in the elevator system and to farmers who store wheat on their farms.
Third, I suggest that a system of advance payments should be adopted so as to give to each producer in western Canada the same income per acre as his neighbour, irrespective of what quotas may exist at the end of the crop year.
Fourth, the government should adopt a system of parity prices that would guarantee the people engaged in the agricultural industry 100 per cent parity of income as compared with people engaged in comparable occupations.
Fifth, I suggest that in order to improve exports of Canadian grain we should be prepared to accept local currencies of countries willing to buy our grain.
Sixth, I suggest that Canada should stand prepared to make bilateral trade contracts in order to guarantee good customers for Canadian wheat that Canada in turn will be a good customer for their commodities.
I submit that if this type of program were adopted it would greatly increase Canadian sales of wheat; it would restore Canada's position in the international markets of the world, and it would bring to our wheat producers a quality of income as compared with people in other industries.

Mr. Speaker, we in the Social Credit group will support the second reading of Bill No. 9, to extend the operations of the wheat board as the sole marketing agency for wheat for another five years. There is no doubt that the majority of farmers do support the wheat board as the sole marketing agency for their grain, and they are asking that flax and rye should be brought under the act. I suggest that the main reason for that is that rye and flax are under quota now. A wide variation in prices has developed, and the farmers want to have the same stability in the marketing of those grains that they have in the marketing of wheat, oats and barley under 1he wheat board.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
I think we are fortunate in the type of men we have had at the head of the wheat board, and I have in mind particularly Mr. Mclvor.
I think it speaks very well that in spite of the difficult times the grain growers have been going through the wheat board is still endorsed by them as the sole marketing agency for their grain. I think the reason for that is that the farmers realize their difficulties are not due to the fact that their grain is marketed through the wheat board, but rather to the failure of the government to cope with the difficult problem of surpluses.
Hon. members on all sides of the house have stressed the fact that agriculture is a depressed industry. It has been stated on many occasions that the net income in 1955 was down 45 per cent from 1951. I am well aware of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture does not consider that a fair comparison because the 1951 income was at the peak; but it is also interesting to note, as has been pointed out by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, that today farm prices are 6 per cent lower than they were in 1949, while farm costs are 20 per cent higher. That indicates the type of cost-price squeeze the farmers are in. No one can suggest that farm prices in 1949 were anywhere near their peak; they were at a quite reasonable level.
In my opinion the depressed condition of agriculture is due largely, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, to the number of large crops harvested in the west. It is due in part also to the fact that we have lost certain markets to the United States, which has resulted in surpluses which in turn have had a depressing effect upon prices. I think the important question that must be dealt with is just how much production do we want. Does the government want a high level of production maintained? From the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that would certainly appear to be the case, and I think he is right.
It will be remembered that last year he said he hoped we would have a bumper crop in 1956. Well, we did have a bumper crop, which helped to increase the problem of the government in marketing.
And the problem of the farmers.

They blame the wheat board for the situation sometimes, but I really do not think the fault lies there at all. The minister has said some rather harsh things about the Gordon commission. I frankly admit that I did not like the report of the Gordon commission so far as agriculture is concerned. I think there are some good points in it and there are some poor ones, but at least at one point the Gordon commission does recognize the fact that the farmers should have some assurance that they will be able to get a minimum income. In other words, they say that when it is agreed that a certain quota should be in force, the wheat board should pay the farmers for the undelivered grain if the board is not in a position to accept delivery of that quota. If that policy had been in force last July it would have gone a long way to do away with the complaint that was being made at that time. I think the government should give serious consideration to a policy of that kind; that is to say, if by July 31 it is not possible to equalize quotas, then advances should be made to the farmers on the grain that has not been delivered in line with the top quotas.
On the question of support prices, we in the Social Credit group for a number of years have been advocating the adoption of the two-price system. We have been advocating it ever since 1950. When we first advocated such a system we pointed out that it is in line with the general practice of secondary industries. Secondary industries set a price for the products sold in Canada at a level that will give them a fair return on their investment. Then on the goods they ship abroad they seek to get the best price they can.
There are times when those goods which are shipped abroad are sold at a price lower than that for which the goods are sold in Canada. I remember that some years ago I checked on the sales of farm machinery by


a Canadian manufacturer, and I found that in England they were selling their machines at prices considerably lower than those at which they were selling the same machines in Canada. In other words, they were operating under a two-price system.
It seems only reasonable that a similar system should be adopted by agriculture. Apart from wheat, about 94 per cent of all farm products is sold in Canada, but we allow that small 6 per cent that is exported abroad to set the price for the other 94 per cent. It appears to me that there is little sense or reason in allowing a situation of that kind to exist. Therefore those people who advocate the adoption of the two-price system are merely advocating that the farm products sold in the domestic market should be sold at parity, or in other words at a price that bears a fair relationship to the prices of other commodities; and that that portion exported abroad should be sold, preferably under international agreement, for the best price that can be obtained, with a support under it to insure the exporter against a price collapse.
It is interesting to note that today every major farm organization is advocating the adoption of a two-price system. At the western agricultural conference held in Winnipeg from January 21 to January 25 this resolution was adopted:
A two-price system establishing prices on all farm products at a fair relationship level for the domestic market and floor prices at non-incentive levels.
It will go the Canadian Federation of Agriculture from that conference. Then the Alberta wheat pool, according to the Wheat Pool Budget, issue of December 14, 1956, stated this:
Two Price System
Alberta wheat pool delegates have passed a resolution calling for a two-price system of selling wheat. They urged that wheat used for domestic consumption in Canada be sold at the ceiling level of the international wheat agreement, namely, $2 a bushel, and that exports be made at world prices which are somewhat below this level.
The Saskatchewan wheat pool advocate a domestic price for wheat used in Canada for human consumption in line with other Canadian prices-that is $2 a bushel-and then deficiency payments from the treasury of Canada to bring the agricultural producers a fair share of the national income when the prices of farm produce do not achieve that end. The exports would be supported. The interprovincial farm union council, in a brief which they put before the federal-provincial agricultural conference, December 3-6, 1956, had this to say:

Parity Prices
We believe that immediate consideration should be given to a program of parity prices on the domestic market and adequate support prices under exports.
In other words they are advocating that the domestic market should pay a parity price and that the world market price with adequate supports be accepted for that portion that has to be exported abroad.
I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce has taken quite strong exception to that suggestion. When the interprovincial farm union council appeared before the committee on agriculture and colonization on June 17, 1952, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, commenting on the proposal to apply the two-price system to wheat, had this to say as reported on page 538 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee:
I can make it plain that as a matter of government policy the Canadian government will not tax the consumers of this country to bonus the wheat producers of western Canada.
Let me point out that the domestic price at parity is no more a tax than is the price charged by secondary industries. They charge a price that gives them fair return on their investment.
More than fair.

Under parity prices the
farmer would receive a price that bore a fair relationship to the prices of secondary industries, so that by no stretch of the imagination could you call that a tax.
Let me point out that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is on somewhat dangerous ground when he suggests that a policy of that kind would be a tax on the consumers of this country. The government did not hesitate to tax the wheat growers some years ago for the benefit of the Canadian consumers. Let us remember that during the operation of the British wheat agreement the western grain growers were compelled to sell their wheat or to have their wheat sold to the millers for the Canadian consumer at a price considerably below the world market price, a price which was at the same level as under the British wheat agreement. That action of subsidizing the Canadian consumer at that time cost the farmers of western Canada $136 million.
Some people say they do not think the farmers are justified in expecting the people of Canada to agree to support prices of agricultural products. There are a number of reasons why the farmers are entitled to that support price. One can go back to 1943, the time at which the ceilings were placed on 82715-58
products, and recall that the then prime minister stated as follows:
If, to help win the war, the farmers are asked to accept a ceiling on prices, we believe they are entitled to a floor under prices to ensure them against an agricultural depression after the war. As an essential part of its post-war policy, the government intends to ask parliament at the next session to place a floor under the prices of main farm commodities.
Would anybody suggest that wheat is not one of the main farm products in this country? Yet strangely enough there is no support price under wheat today because wheat is not covered by the agricultural Prices Support Act.
One might ask whether or not the price of wheat today is a fair one. In the first place, what would parity be? If the price of wheat today were maintained at parity level, according to the bureau of statistics- and I obtained these figures last week-it would be $2.37 a bushel. That is to say, if the formula that is used under the Agricultural Prices Support Act were used to cover wheat, the price would be $2.37 a bushel.
Let us recall that under the Agricultural Prices Support Act we use the base period 1943, 1944 and 1945, and then say the price of farm products today should bear the same relationship to the prices of other commodities as they existed in the 1943, 1944 and 1945 period. If that were put into execution in regard to wheat prices, wheat today would be $2.37 a bushel. Instead of that, the price of No. 1 wheat to the farmer is, I suppose, around $1.53 by the time you pay the freight to Fort William, or $1.70 at Fort William. So when you compare the price farmers are getting for their wheat with parity prices we find there is a very substantial difference, and that the farmers are losing quite heavily in regard to the promise that was made by the prime minister back in 1943.
Whilst the price of No. 1 wheat is about $1.70, let hon. members not forget that many farmers today, in order to try to get some income are selling their wheat for as low as 60 or 65 cents a bushel in western Canada, that is No. 5 or No. 6 wheat. If a farmer is up against it and cann*t sell his wheat to the elevators, then he looks around for a market for his feed wheat. He can sell his feed wheat if he takes 60 or 65 cents a bushel for it, but that is a heavy loss the farmer should not have to take. It is a loss he would not have to take if the government would introduce a policy of advances against grain stored on the farm.

In the Western Producer of December 13, 1956, there is a quotation taken from the Financial Post. I shall read it.
Finance Minister Walter Harris deserves a good deal of credit for speaking plainly on an important subject in Toronto last week. He came out clearly and strongly against a policy of government farm price supports. "We are close enough to the American experience", said Mr. Harris, "to realize that certain policies offer no solution to our problems."
It is quite a popular pastime with certain ministers of this government to criticize the policies of the United States under which surplus products have been marketed. I would say that the program in the United States, instead of being a failure, has been a gigantic success when you realize the purpose behind it. Let us go back to the end of the war and the Hot Springs conference of FAO, when apparently we all had high ideals. Let us recall the declaration that was made at that time by the member nations, and let me quote section No. 3:
There has never been enough food for the health of all people. This is justified neither by ignorance nor by the harshness of nature. Production of food must be greatly expanded; we now have knowledge of the means by which this can be done. It requires imagination and firm will on the part of each government and people to make use of that knowledge.
That was back in 1943, I think. I believe we will all agree that the United States addressed themselves to that problem. They took energetic action to build up their production, and they were successful in building it up. They built it up at a faster rate than the FAO or other United Nations organizations were able to distribute it.
The FAO did a lot of very valuable work in trying to establish an organization which would have the responsibility for distributing surplus food to. needy nations. First of all we had the suggestion for a world food board. Then we had the suggestion for an international commodity clearing house, and I think that was the best suggestion put forward by the FAO organization.
The Canadian government, along with others, turned down the proposal. I would say that probably one of the main reasons they turned it down was that it embodied the idea of the acceptance of foreign currency in payment for surpluses. In any event, the FAO were not successful in getting other 
nations to accept their proposals, and consequently each nation was left with the responsibility of disposing of its surpluses. The United States, in carrying out the request of the FAO to build up their production, had built up tremendous surpluses, and these surpluses were left on their doorstep.
On the other side of the picture you had half the population of the world hungry or on the verge of starvation. The United States, and I think it is to their credit, found ways and means of getting that surplus food to the people who needed it. What did we do? Instead of complimenting them upon getting this food to the people who needed it we did nothing but criticize them. Why did we criticize them? We did so from purely selfish reasons, because that action interfered with our own markets. I would suggest that instead of criticizing the United States for what they have been doing we should be prepared to do likewise, and get our surplus food to the nations that need it.
I should like to refer the Minister of Trade and Commerce to a statement made by Right Hon. A. B. Low, minister of state for the British board of trade, regarding sterling. Pound sterling accepted by Canadian exporters for sales to Britain, can be used for purchases of goods anywhere in the sterling area. Right Hon. A. B. Low, minister of state in the British board of trade, told the Western Producer in an interview at Edmonton last week.
That is all I am going to say on that point now, but that points out that sterling would not be quite such a useless commodity as the Minister of Trade and Commerce tried to make out last year, when he said you could not even buy a necktie with it. Certainly the United States is making its surplus production available to the nations that need it.

We are quite prepared to sell our commodity on the basis of quality any place in the world if we are able to buy those items which enter into the cost of production in a fair market; but it is quite impossible for us to buy in the highest priced market in the world and sell in competition with other countries which are directly and indirectly subsidizing their wheat producers.
The Department of Agriculture publishes a pamphlet called "Agriculture Abroad" every two or three months. The one for December discussed agriculture in a great many countries. I shall refer to a few of them. The price in the Argentine is not too high, but there is a subsidy of 36 cents a bushel there. The hon. member for Assiniboia referred to the situation in France. France is paying a price much higher than our farmers receive. France is determined to be in the export business. It appears that agricultural problems in West Germany have received careful consideration. Plans have been worked out and legislation introduced with a view to greatly increasing West Germany's production, particularly of cereals.
While the position of the Mexican farmer resembles the position of the Canadian farmer and those in a few other countries of the world, Mexico is recognizing that her farmers are receiving a pretty rough deal. Approximately 30 million people in Mexico make a living by farming; they comprise almost 60 per cent of the total population, and receive about 30 per cent of the national income.

That is running pretty true to form as far as Canada is concerned. The Mexican farmer receives about half as much as he should receive. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that when the' authorities in the very rich country to the south recognize that they have a farm problem; when they bring in legislation to provide money for a soil bank program and carry on barter sales and negotiate for the acceptance of soft currencies, the Minister of Trade and Commerce who is piloting this measure through the house should not be too complacent. He should not be satisfied because this is the best marketing agency that has been devised in Canada or anywhere in the world. The legislation must be tested and weighed against the question as to whether it is doing everything that reasonably can be expected.
I notice that it is five o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I would like to continue my remarks at a later period.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 9, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.

Mr. Speaker, some reference was made this afternoon to the preliminary report of the Gordon commission. I do not think anyone agrees with everything in the report, but it is significant that it was considered necessary to devote a separate section to wheat. I think it is disturbing that the best authorities seem to accept the fact that Canada's part in supplying wheat for bread for the hungry peoples of the world is not going to increase. I think most people throughout the world had hoped that in the brave new world which followed the second world war we would attack in an imaginative way the problem of hunger, and that our great wheat fields would be cultivated and food would be sent to those other countries.
The forecast is that our combined export and domestic demand will be between 400 million and 500 million bushels per annum, compared with 385 million bushels in the 20's; 330 million bushels in the 30's; 393 million bushels in the 40's; and an average of 525 million bushels during the seven years 1950-56. It is true that the target of between 400 million and 475 million bushels is a good deal more than our total when the Canadian and world populations were much smaller, but I think it is disturbing that apparently there is going to be no attempt to reach the average established in 1950-56 of 525 million bushels per year.
The federal authorities should make a decision well in advance of seeding as to the quantity of grain which would be expected, and it should decide something about the price. I would remind the house that the minister who is piloting this bill through the house is also charged with defence production. Some time ago he told us that the CF-105 was going to cost $120 million. Apparently he was wrong, because we are now told it will cost over $200 million before

the first CF-105 comes off the assembly line. We are told that in connection with guided missiles we had spent some $24 million when it was concluded that this was too big a project for Canada, that it would be left to the United States to spend money on the development of guided missiles. We have recently completed the construction of the mid-Canada radar line at a cost of another $200 million.
It seems to me that if this minister is prepared to spend $200 million for a plane and $2C0 million for a radar line, he could ask his colleagues to use their imagination in order that Canada may not go out of the production and exporting of this important commodity, which in my view could be used more effectively in winning friends for the free countries. I think the proposal that the farmer should have some indication as to what the requirements are going to be and how much the economy will stand is a good one.
It is disturbing to be told that our farm population, which stood at 25 per cent of the total at the end of the war, is now reduced to 15 per cent and will be further reduced to about half that in the next 25 years. I submit that the minister in his capacity of minister in charge of the wheat board should give the board the green light to make arrangements with Canadian farmers so they may continue to produce sufficient food to meet our own requirements and to permit us to make some impression on the problem of hunger which has confronted over one billion people throughout the world all their lives, and which is likely to continue during the life of most of us here.
I think the question of bringing goods into Canada from the countries which are buying our wheat must also be considered in connection with the extension of the life of the wheat board. I believe most members will recognize what an impossible task the members of the board are going to have if they are going to be required to dispose of wheat in countries that are prepared to accept our wheat on condition that we purchase some of their goods. Last year the minister was able to end the year in quite a favourable position partly because of the very substantial sales made to Russia and some of the other iron curtain countries. The last time I discussed the question of wheat in the house I referred to our sales to Poland, and pointed out that Poland is apparently planning on buying upward of 20 million bushels of wheat per year over the next 10 years. Apparently Poland is well satisfied with the quality of our wheat and is prepared to give us a fair share of their imports.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
It would appear that last year Poland bought around $20 million worth of wheat, over $1 million worth of rye and about $250,000 worth of barley, total purchases in Canada amounting to $25 million. But what about our purchases from Poland? They are running around $2 million. The proposal made last year by Poland was that if we could buy around $5 million worth of goods from Poland they would be prepared to use scarce dollars to buy around $10 million worth of goods a year from Canada.
But surely that is not a concern entirely for the people of Poland. Surely the Minister of Trade and Commerce has some responsibility to give some encouragement and direction to these customers of ours who are not going to be able to continue to purchase agricultural products if more interest is not taken in their products.
The same thing goes for Great Britain. Great Britain has been one of our very best customers, but there has been no serious attempt to see that the wheat board or any other organization is charged with some responsibility for seeing that more British goods find a market in Canada. Therefore it would seem to me that the minister must accept the responsibility for setting up an import board which will have similar responsibilities to those of the wheat board. I am not suggesting that the government should accept a policy which would be foreign to them, but I think if the government set up an import board which could place the problem in its proper perspective before the Canadian people it would be fairly easy to decrease our purchases of goods in markets where we have an unfavourable balance, and increase our purchases of goods in countries where we bought so little.
I submit that the minister must give consideration immediately to the setting up of an import board to deal with the problem of getting goods into Canada from our good customers in the past and from our new customers. Last year, as I said, we sold about $20 million worth of wheat to Poland. I cannot see any reason why in a sale of this sort it is necessary for our customers to go to the brokers or agents on the grain exchange. I understand that there would be a commission of one-half of 1 per cent. It would appear to me that would be something like $100,000 on one sale alone.
Since the wheat board seems to be able to set up very efficient machinery to buy wheat in 1-bushel lots, 5-bushel lots or 10-bushel lots from any farmer regardless of the amount he has to sell, I see no reason
