Canadian Wheat Board Act under the sun why the same organization cannot sell this product directly to those customers who would prefer to buy directly from the wheat board. I suggest that the splitting of this $100,000 commission on one transaction alone so the buyer might have half and the seller might have half would meet with very general approval on the part of the farmers, who need every last cent they can get. I submit that taking $100,000 of their hard-earned money to complete a sale through brokers or agents is not in the best interest of producers or consumers.
Having listened to speakers from all parties who are anxious that the method of marketing through the wheat board should continue, I submit that the minister should give consideration to following the same procedure he followed two years ago in connection with the Defence Production Act, and introduce legislation to provide that the wheat board act will be made permanent.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the main purpose of the bill now before us is to extend for another five years the provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. In Saskatchewan the socialists say the Liberal party has no selling policy for marketing wheat. I want to emphasize that this act is the very cornerstone of Liberal marketing policy. In a nutshell, the bill provides that the wheat board shall continue to be the main marketing agency for wheat, barley and oats. I believe I am correct in saying that 99 per cent of prairie farmers, regardless of their politics, support the bill in principle.
It is quite true that world conditions have strained the facilities of the board in the last five years. It is also quite true that our bins, granaries and elevators in western Canada are jammed to capacity at this moment with about a billion bushels of unsold wheat. But this situation was not caused by a breakdown in the selling machinery. Rather I think the wheat surplus has been caused by three other factors. First, as the minister pointed out this afternoon, we have had an unprecedented series of bumper crops. Second, there is the fact that many former importing countries, helped by United States aid and machinery, have in recent years become exporting countries. Third, there is the terrific competition of American giveaway programs.
Despite all these difficulties the Canadian wheat board has steadily, patiently and without panic continued to sell wheat in the world markets at the best possible price for the producer. Personally I think the wheat board has done an excellent job in the past five years. Our export movement of wheat 

has never fallen below the long-term average. The last crop year was one of the most satisfactory export years we have ever had in our history. A vigorous selling campaign was carried on by the wheat board and the government in the iron curtain countries as well as in our traditional markets, and so successful was that drive that last year we exported 309 million bushels of wheat, an increase of 57 million bushels over a year ago.
What is even more encouraging to the western farmer at this moment is the fact that up to January 15 of the current year our exports have been 108.5 million bushels compared with only 71.1 million bushels a year ago, an increase of about 42 per cent. It was said this afternoon that we have lost some of our markets to the United States. Most of those markets were lost primarily, if they were lost, because the Americans gave wheat away.
I sincerely believe that during the past several years the wheat board has done a good job, not only because it sold a great deal of wheat but also because it prevented the price of wheat from dropping very substantially.
A few weeks ago Mr. J. H. Wesson, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, was speaking in Regina. From the Leader-Post I quote what he said on that occasion:
"Other problems which we have considered at this meeting . . . are small in comparison to the danger which we have passed through that wheat prices might have fallen by 50 to 75 cents during the past year."
Then the report continues:
He urged delegates to tell the membership that the wheat board and the international wheat agreement had averted this catastrophe.
Those are the main reasons the Liberal members from Saskatchewan are 100 per cent behind the Canadian wheat board in their effort to get a better price for the producer. However, I find it most difficult to understand the attitude of the socialist members from Saskatchewan toward the Canadian wheat board. On the one hand they solemnly profess vigorously to support the wheat board in all its objectives, yet on the other hand here in parliament and out on the hustings the socialists criticize just about everything the wheat board does.
What, for example?
They say that selling policies are ineffective, that the allocation of quotas at delivery points are unfair.
What about cash advances?

The board members said
they did not want advances. The socialists

say we should have them. They say the wheat board are subservient to the government.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the hon. member a question.
Certainly.
Does the hon. member agree that the quotas that apply on box cars at individual loading points have been fair to the prairie province producers?

I say that the quotas at delivery points have not been all the farmers might wish. But I also say the Canadian wheat board, when all circumstances are considered, has done the best possible job it could.
Mr. Speaker, I would be the last one in the world to say that the prairie farmer has not laboured under great difficulty in these past few years. Of course it is disheartening and discouraging to grow one bumper crop after another and find it possible to sell only a portion of it. But I also say that the lot of the farmer is not made easier in Saskatchewan by the socialist members who since 1945 have acted in this house as professional cry-babies.
You are including yourself.

They have wept copious tears. They have cried blue ruin. They have preached gloom. They have prophesied disaster, and time and again they have forecast a complete collapse of world wheat markets. All through Saskatchewan they have tried to stir up trouble by exaggerations and statements which frequently border on untruths. For example, here is one statement which the hon. member for Assiniboia made when speaking at the convention of the hon. member for Mackenzie, and I quote dispatches from the Regina Leader-Post which I presume the hon. member for Assiniboia himself sent in:
Mr. Argue emphasized that at the present time the farmers . . . are in as serious a condition as they were in the thirties.
Mr. Speaker, in the thirties wheat was selling at as low as 20 cents a bushel; eggs were selling for as little as 5 cents a dozen; the price of cattle was as low as $10 a head. People in those days had to depend on eastern Canada for charity, for their clothing and even for food. Yet the hon. member for Assiniboia says that conditions are as bad today as they were in the 1930's.

Today their share of the national income is less.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
The people out in Saskatchewan have too much sense to believe that statement.
Have you compared the farmers' income?

According to the dominion bureau of statistics, in 1931 cash income for Saskatchewan farm products was $74 million; in 1932 it was $80 million; in 1933 it was $80 million; in 1934 it was $96.5 million. Last year the cash income for Saskatchewan farm products was $592.7 million.
That is a typical Liberal trick.
Yet the hon. member for Assiniboia says the farmers are as badly off as they were in the thirties.
Give the net farm income.

Mr. Speaker, there is no one so blind as he who refuses to see. I am not going to try to tell this house that the prairie farmer is satisfied with everything the Canadian wheat board does. He is not. However, I am going to say this. The Saskatchewan farmer is a rugged individualist who is fiercely independent in his way of life. He is proud of his province; he is proud of his country, and he is proud of his own accomplishments in farming since 1945. He wants every dollar that is fairly and justly coming to him. Above all he does not want to be pushed around by the more populous provinces. But despite the wailings and snivellings of the C.C.F. here in this house he wants no charity or hand-outs from any one. In talking about wheat selling policies, I say that many of these socialists have taken an attitude that has harmed the producer instead of helping him.
Nonsense.

By their talk in parliament, by their complete lack of financial responsibility, by their lack of any constructive suggestions, the socialists have injured the prestige and welfare of the province of Saskatchewan. Mr. Speaker, they have cried "Wolf" so often that when one of them gets to his feet hon. members from other parts of Canada are immediately suspicious and automatically hostile.
It may be that some westerners think that I am exaggerating when I make that statement. Here is a quotation from Hansard showing what happened in debate on March 13, 1956. As reported at page 2100 the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Bennett), who was then speaking, had this to say:
I should like to say this to the C.C.F. group. I came down here prepared and anxious to help the

Canadian Wheat Board Act western farmer. After hearing all the repetitious debates that took place here, I was reluctant to vote for those bills. I think the western farmer has not had the kind of representation here that he deserves.
From the 12 years I have spent in this parliament, Mr. Speaker, I am absolutely convinced that the western farmer will get more by a spirit of reasonableness and cooperation on the part of members representing him than he will by the constant stream of abuse and vituperation that comes from the socialist group.
Why did you not give the farmers of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre a chance to express their opinion?

The Canadian wheat board is responsible for selling the nation's wheat. The socialists from Saskatchewan usually lack the courage to come out directly and attack the wheat board. Instead, they go after the government, saying that in actual fact it is responsible for its policy. I pose this question to the house today. Could the socialist members from Saskatchewan do any better than the government or the wheat board are doing in selling this billion bushels of wheat? I submit that they could not, if we are to judge from their experiences in other fields. Surely there is no better way in which to judge an individual or a political group than by their accomplishments. I do not pay so much attention to talk and words as I do to the past record. What are the accomplishments of the socialists in the field of selling? Out in Saskatchewan, Mr. Speaker, back in 1945 the provincial C.C.F. government embarked on a number of crown corporations.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a
point of order.
Sit down and take it.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say that-

speechtext: The brick plant.

-last year, the hon.
member discussed crown corporations in the pipeline debate and the Liberals refused me an opportunity to reply. I submit that the hon. member should not be allowed to discuss Saskatchewan crown corporations at this time unless ample opportunity is given to put forward the other side of the question.
On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I do not blame the hon. member for Mackenzie for not wanting that record put on Hansard, but may I submit-
Oh, oh.

-here are our socialist friends coming into this parliament and saying that the wheat board does not know anything about selling a billion bushel wheat surplus. I want to put on Hansard two or three illustrations of the socialist selling record in Saskatchewan.
On the point of order, Mr. Speaker,-
We do not want to hear it.
-I want to hear from the Speaker as to whether or not a discussion of crown corporations in Saskatchewan is in order on this bill?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The
debate we have had this afternoon, from start to finish, has ranged far afield. Shortly before five o'clock I was in considerable difficulty as to whether or not I should not then have intervened because of references- I do not remember them exactly-to aeroplane production, the cost of the D.E.W. line and so forth. In an honest effort to rule always in favour of whoever had the floor, I considered that references to other things- this happened to be a reference to a series of matters which had come under the control of the minister who was responsible for this bill-were getting us far afield from the wheat board, but I think perhaps the references were fair. If the hon. member who has the floor now proposes to make certain references to show that those who oppose the bill have, by a similar line of action, indicated their ability or inability to take wise action, I do not think I should stop that either. But I have no intention of permitting the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre to go farther than to make the same type of reference or listing of what he considers comparable matters as has been done in previous speeches made in this debate.
I believe the house will agree with me that it has been the desire of the house this afternoon that matters directly and indirectly affecting the wheat board should be discussed under this bill. One could, of course, have made a very narrow ruling that nothing could be discussed except shall or shall not the wheat board be extended and if so, shall it be for a period of five years. I do not believe it was the sense of the house that this should be the ruling, but I shall continue to endeavour to keep members within what I think is the general ambit of the subject under debate, having gone as it has gone so far. I do not think comparable references should be ruled out all of a sudden, when they have been permitted in the last two or three speeches.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I wanted to endeavour to explain to the house how unsuccessful the socialists have been in selling other products out in the province of Saskatchewan, so we can then judge their ability to sell a billion bushels of wheat in the most competitive market in the world.
You did that in the pipeline debate last year.

I shall only give a few examples for purposes of comparison. In 1945 they set up a leather tannery. We certainly had lots of hides out in Saskatchewan, and the crown company was able to turn out a large amount of leather. Unfortunately they did not have salesmen who could sell this leather effectively in the country's markets, so the company folded. They started a shoe factory in the city of Regina and manufactured thousands and thousands of pairs of shoes. Unfortunately again, apparently they did not have salesmen who could sell those shoes in competition with other companies. This company was also forced to close its doors.
Out in my own city of Moose Jaw they set up a woollen mill. The woollen mill operated fairly actively for a while and turned out a great many woollen goods. They did not have the salesmen who could sell these goods competitively and were forced to close. I could go on for quite some time in listing these illustrations-
What did you say about the closing of the woollen mill at that time?

-but I suppose that someone could take exception. I do want to say this in summing up, Mr. Speaker, that in the province of Saskatchewan, out of all the crown corporations that were set up, and which had to compete with private interprise, there was not one that had good enough salesmen, to be able to compete effectively without losing substantial sums of the taxpayers' money, or close their doors entirely.
That is not true, and you know it.

The great majority of the crown corporations have some kind of monopoly or some kind of special privilege. But even where they have arbitrarily taken special privileges, their salesmen have not been able to compete efficiently. I mention the field of gas. A complete monopoly is what those salesmen have, yet the price they charge for gas in Saskatchewan is more than double the price of gas under private enterprise in our sister province of Alberta.
Most socialists have had very little to do with the business world; most of them are not
Canadian Wheat Board Act very well acquainted with commerce. There have been one or two notable exceptions. For example, several years ago our premier and provincial treasurer went into the drive-in theatre business. The theatre went pretty well for a while, but then suddenly it folded. Today it stands empty and desolate, a monument to the failure of the premier and his chief lieutenant to sell the people of Regina on the merits of their particular enterprise.
They cannot even entertain the people.

I say that the record of socialist salesmanship in Saskatchewan is a record of ineptitude, inefficiency and bungling. Yet these socialists today have the audacity to say something like this in parliament: It is true that we could not sell blankets or textiles out in Saskatchewan; it is a fact that we could not sell hides or shoes; it is true that in the middle of the greatest construction boom Canada has ever had we are having some considerable difficulty in selling our bricks; it is a fact we could not sell timber, gas, fish, or furs without a monopoly, and it is also true-
Nonsense.

-we need certain special privileges to sell our insurance. As a matter of fact, it is true that out in Saskatchewan we could not sell anything efficiently. But let no one be worried. By national planning and socialist theories, we could sell a billion bushels of wheat overnight.
You are going to have trouble selling yourself.

Socialist planning means
that the provincial government usually takes some teacher or preacher or someone who knows nothing about business, and puts him in charge of an enterprise. These socialists today are telling us in effect that men like McNamara, Mclvor, Riddel, C. D. Howe and James G. Gardiner do not know anything about selling wheat. But, they say, let us be the salesmen and we would get rid of a billion bushels of wheat. I would say that the practical farmer in Saskatchewan has far too much sense to listen to such nonsense.
Why don't you tell that to the farmers in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre?

During the past few months
I have had many farmers come into my office to tell me about their problems in connection with wheat.

From Moose Jaw-Lake
Centre?

Canadian Wheat Board Act

Yes. I told you once before that experience is a great teacher, and it is an extremely foolish man who will not learn from experience. I, fortunately, learned a little, but my hon. friend did not.
Most of these farmers, when they come into my office, talk about wheat. I ask them, it they were the Prime Minister, what they could do about the surpluses, or what solution they might suggest. They are usually frank enough to admit that they have no over-all solution to offer. The reason they have not is rather obvious. Today, regardless of what any member in this house says, there is not an easy solution or a pat answer or a magic formula.
What are some of the proposals which have been put forward over the past four or five years by our socialists? Most of them, I suggest, are little more than economic nonsense. We heard some of them this afternoon. The first suggestion, made year after year, is that Canada should give away the wheat surplus. The hon. member for Assiniboia has been particularly vociferous in putting forward that suggestion. I suggest to you that if the government had followed that proposal from the time it was first made, a number of years ago, the taxpayers today would be several billion dollars poorer. I am constantly amazed at the willingness of my former socialist colleagues to give away money which belongs to someone else, or give away assets which belong to others. They are never so generous with their own possessions.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We gave you away.

Frankly, I feel that Canada should not hesitate to make gifts of wheat to the starving countries of the world. We are doing that under the Colombo plan; but to suggest sincerely that we should take several billions of dollars, put it into wheat and give that wheat away, I do not think is practical. Surely federal representatives in this house should be just as responsible in spending the taxpayers' money as they are in spending their own. I do not think there is one socialist in the house who would dream of spending his own money in that reckless manner, including the hon. member for Assiniboia. I suggest that if the hon. member for Assiniboia does feel that the Christian and humanitarian thing for Canada to do is to give away our wheat, he should set the example and give his own crop away. It is easy, Mr. Speaker, to be generous with someone else's money.
The second suggestion which has been made frequently by the socialists is that the government and the wheat board should take


sterling in return for wheat. Well, that suggestion may sound plausible, but actually it is not much more practical than their first scheme. Out in Saskatoon, about a year and three months ago, the British trade commissioner was invited to speak to a farm union meeting. One of the delegates rose and asked this question:
If Canada would take sterling would we sell any more wheat to Great Britain?
According to the report of the meeting appearing in the Regina Leader-Post of December 2, 1955, Mr. Bowen made this flat reply:
Britain would not purchase a bushel more if sterling were accepted in payment by Canada.
I think the trade commissioner's statement indicates the value of that socialist suggestion.
Well, now, socialists say in parliament and they say around the country that we should accept local currency in payment for wheat. What this really means, of course, is that we should sell our wheat at a discount, because if the local currency is as good as dollars then there is no difficulty in selling for dollars. If the local currency is not as good as dollars then, in fact, the wheat is being sold at a discount. Personally I doubt whether the western farmer would welcome a lower price for wheat than he is getting at the present time, yet that would inevitably happen unless the federal treasury were prepared to make up the difference by subsidy.
Another favourite proposition put forth by socialist members is that we should barter our wheat. I notice that whenever they talk in this manner they talk in generalities; they are never specific. I have nothing against barter when somebody comes forward with a sensible proposition, but so far no socialist has done that.

The
hon. member knows no more about wheat than he knows about Mae West.

The socialists are never specific as to what countries want to barter with us, nor about the goods we can get in return for our wheat. If they were specific about barter the western farmers would realize that it would have the same effect on the wheat surplus as a pail of water taken from the Saskatchewan river would have in lowering its level.
The fourth suggestion put forward by socialists from time to time-I cite the speech of the hon. member for Assiniboia on May 17, 1955-is that the government should provide a school lunch program to take care of further agricultural surpluses. Well, I am not going into the merits or demerits of that

plan, except to say that a school lunch program would have the same effect on our wheat surplus as a workman would have trying to dig the St. Lawrence seaway with a teaspoon.
The fifth suggestion that has come again from the hon. member for Assiniboia is that there should be a march on Ottawa. Well, I say that a march on Ottawa at this time would be the work of a few professional socialist agitators organized for the sole purpose of trying to make political capital out of the farmers' difficulties. I believe that members in this house of all political parties, even the socialist group, want the farmer to be treated fairly and justly. I do not think they have to be pressured into giving him fair treatment by a march like the socialists have suggested. I say that C.C.F. members from their leader down to their remotest backbencher have so far offered no real solution for our wheat surplus problem.
I listened to the socialist members speak this afternoon. I hoped they would tell us how they would sell more wheat than is already being sold. Not one sensible, concrete suggestion was put forward.
I conclude by quoting a Canadian Press dispatch from Winnipeg, and again it is Mr. Wesson speaking:
The Canadian wheat board averted a possible international economic crisis and saved the situation for the farmer, John Wesson, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, told the western agricultural conference here.
I think these words of Mr. Wesson justify Liberal marketing policy in western Canada, and most effectively answer the criticisms which have come from the socialists today.
I support with enthusiasm the legislation which is now before us, Mr. Speaker, and I want to tell my hon. friends from Saskatchewan on the opposition benches that there are some members in this house who are not keen about the wheat board because they are a little bit afraid it may be a socialist measure. The criticism and unceasing opposition of socialists to the wheat board may result in a situation like this, one of these days. Eastern members are going to say, "All right, fellows, if the wheat board is so bad let us scrap it". That is the situation which these members may provoke. I suggest, whether deliberately or otherwise, they are time and again indirectly sabotaging the Canadian wheat board by irresponsible talk. Today the Liberal government is doing the best possible job under difficult circumstances.

Will the hon. member permit a question before he resumes his seat? Will he suggest some ways of moving more
Canadian Wheat Board Act wheat to give the wheat farmers a fairer share of the national income?

Mr. Speaker, I thought I was very clear in what I said. I believe there is no magic formula. There is no easy answer to this problem; but I do say that the wheat board and the Liberal party are doing their best under difficult world circumstances. They are trying to get the best possible price for the western producer.

I would like to ask the hon. member a question. I do not think he was quite fair in his allusion to the shoe factory and the woollen factory. He is a businessman. Does he consider that private enterprise in the same sort of thing, shoes or woollens, could have succeeded in Saskatchewan? Second, does he not know that these tiny little industries, which have been magnified in the east where, when you talk about a shoe factory, you talk about something big-
Who tried it? The C.C.F.

My question is this. Does he not know that these little factories were simply built at the time of a terrible depression so we would have shoes and wool for our people, if they were necessary? Is it fair for him to say that these things failed in Saskatchewan because of socialist policies? Could these industries ever have succeeded under private enterprise in the province of Saskatchewan?

Well, Mr. Speaker, there was a time when I believed that socialist enterprises were necessary and desirable for my province, but after 10 years' experience I saw the way they operated and most of them went broke. There is quite a difference when a socialist company goes bankrupt and when a private enterprise company goes bankrupt. When a socialist company closes it is the taxpayers' money that has been lost, and millions have been lost in that manner in Saskatchewan. When a private enterprise company closes, the only people who lose are the shareholders.

I wish the hon. member would answer my question. Does he consider that private enterprise on a woollen mill or shoe factory, having regard to business and supply under the circumstances, could have operated successfully in the city of Moose Jaw?
Should we trust that kind of government to sell wheat?

If a private company had closed, the only people who would have lost would have been the shareholders. I do not see any relevancy to that question.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the previous speaker a question. I take it from his remarks that he questions the advisability of an organized march on Ottawa. I would like to know if he would advise the permanent lobby which the farmers' union of Alberta have established down here at the present time.

I would say that I think every hon. member in this house regardless of his politics is sympathetic to the difficulties of the farmers, and I do not believe a march on Ottawa at this time is needed or desirable.

We are not in committee.

I did not object to that. I objected to a march on Ottawa.

1.	What Is the actual cost of old age pension paid entirely by the federal government without means test, for pensioners over 70?
2.	What would be the cost of such pension if the age limit was reduced from 70 to 65 years of age?
3.	What is the amount of the contribution actually paid by the federal government to old age pensioners between the ages of 65 and 70?
4.	What would be the amount of the said contribution if such pension were paid to pensioners of 60 to 65 years of age?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1.	Estimated cost for complete year 1956-57 -$379,375,000.
2.	Estimated cost for complete year 1957-58 -$608,000,000, less $21,100,000 which represents the estimated federal share for 1957-58 of payments under the Old Age Assistance Act.
3.	Estimated cost of the federal share of old age assistance for complete year 1956-57 -$20,500,000.
4.	The cost to the federal government of paying old age assistance to persons 60 to 64 years of age would depend on a number of factors which could vary considerably from those which apply to persons 65 to 69 years of age. A great deal would depend on the requirements of eligibility to be applied, particularly the means test. Presumably a larger proportion of persons 60 to 64 would be employable. The extent to which persons in this age group who were in need of assistance would be assisted by unemployment insurance and unemployment assistance would have an important bearing on the number applying for old age assistance. With so many unpredictable factors it would be difficult to estimate with any degree of accuracy the cost to the federal government of paying old age assistance to persons 60 to 64 years of age.
